**Short answer:** Based on the documents, your landlord or agent probably can't make you pay a card fee when a fee-free option, such as bank transfer, is reasonably available. The documents don't say whether the fee goes to the app company or the agent, and that difference doesn't appear to change the rule.

**Versions in force:** On 15 January 2026, the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (rta-1997-v111-2025-11-25.pdf, dated 25 November 2025, version 111) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf, dated 25 November 2025, version 005) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) were both in force. I'm relying on the version numbers in the documents' metadata.

**What the law says**

- The provider or agent "must ensure that a rent payment method that incurs no additional costs (other than bank fees or account fees payable on the renter's bank account) is reasonably available to the renter" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person or 400 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- Before you agree to a payment method, the provider or agent must tell you about any costs you may incur, including "third party transaction fees" and "any other electronic payment facility fees" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- The provider must allow payment by Centrepay and by a prescribed method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The prescribed method is electronic funds transfer [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- A term in a residential rental agreement that requires the renter to pay rent in advance by a payment method that has additional costs (other than bank or account fees) is a prohibited term [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- Schedule 1 of the regulations notes that the provider "must permit at least one fee-free (other than the renter's own bank fees) payment method" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

**Does it matter who gets the fee?**

The documents don't distinguish between a fee paid to the app company and one paid to the agent. The obligations in section 42(4) fall on the provider "or that person's agent" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The documents don't address whether an app company acting for the agent changes this. I can't confirm that from these documents.

**A rule that doesn't yet apply:** Regulation 21C bans rent payment fees, except payment surcharges permitted under another Act, but it "has effect on and after 31 March 2026" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). It is not in force on 15 January 2026. The documents also don't include the text of section 51A of the Act, which it refers to [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do**

- Ask the provider or agent to confirm in writing that a no-fee method, such as bank transfer, is available, and that you can use it without paying the card fee.
- Ask for the cost information the law requires them to give you before you consent to the card option [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- If you pay by bank transfer, you can request a written receipt. For a payment not made in person, it must be given "within 5 business days of receiving the payment" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't describe how to make a complaint or what the Tribunal process is, so I can't advise on those steps from these sources.

answer:
**Short answer:** Under the law in force on 15 October 2019, you can likely cancel if you haven't moved in, and you can require repairs. The documents don't give you a right to reduce rent for these defects.

**Governing version:** The *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 088 (file rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf, in force from 2 July 2019 to 3 December 2019), applies on your date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). It uses the newer terms "residential rental provider" (landlord) and "renter" (tenant) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

---

### What the law says

- **Condition on move-in:** The provider must ensure the premises are vacant and in a reasonably clean condition on the agreed day you enter occupation. If they aren't, you are not required to move in, and you don't have to pay rent for the period before you actually move in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). This section is about cleanliness, so it doesn't clearly cover damp or rot.
- **Minimum standards:** The provider must ensure the premises comply with prescribed rental minimum standards on or before the day you enter occupation (penalty: 60 penalty units for an individual, 300 for a body corporate). If they don't comply on or just after that day, you may request urgent repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The documents do not include the content of these standards.
- **Good repair:** The provider must keep the premises in good repair and reasonably fit and suitable for occupation. This applies even if you knew of the disrepair before moving in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Mould and damp:** "Urgent repairs" includes "the presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure," and any fault that makes the premises unsafe or insecure [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether rotting timber counts as unsafe.

---

### What you can do

**1. Cancel**
- If you have not entered possession and you give the landlord notice of termination on the ground that the premises are not in good repair or are unfit for human habitation, the tenancy terminates [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- Check first whether picking up the keys counts as taking possession. If it does, this route may not apply.
- The documents don't state a notice period for this termination.

**2. Ask for repairs**
- **Notify in writing:** Give written notice as soon as practicable after you become aware of the damage or breakdown [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). If you receive a condition report, it counts as notice of any defects it states [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). If you were not given one, you may complete one and give it to the provider within the period between inspecting the premises and 5 business days after moving in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs:** If you have taken reasonable steps to get the provider to repair immediately and they can't, you may arrange the repairs. The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days after written notice of the repairs and their cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs at the Tribunal (VCAT):** You can apply if you can't meet the cost, the repairs cost more than the prescribed amount, or the provider refuses to pay. The Tribunal must hear the application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Non-urgent repairs:** If repairs aren't done within 14 days after your written notice, you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring specified repairs. The Tribunal must hear the application within 7 days and may order that a suitably qualified person carry out the work [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Rent into the Rent Special Account:** If you have given notice and the provider has failed to carry out repairs, you may apply for an order that your rent be paid into the Rent Special Account. The Tribunal must make the order unless the provider shows financial hardship [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**3. Ask for lower rent**
- The documents do not contain a provision allowing you to reduce rent because of these defects.
- The closest provisions are the no-rent-before-move-in rule described above [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) and the Director's power to investigate rent that is excessive, which is tied to reduced services or a proposed rent increase [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Neither clearly provides a rent reduction in your situation.
- Holding rent in the Rent Special Account [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) is not a reduction.

---

**Next steps:** Put your complaint in writing now, with photos, and keep a copy. Then decide whether to cancel or require repairs, and consider taking advice from VCAT or Consumer Affairs Victoria before acting. This summary is based only on the Act text retrieved and is not legal advice.

**Short answer:** The documents do not say whether you must personally be present, and they do not address a $90 rebooking fee. They do set out the entry rules that apply, and you can negotiate the time.

**Which law applies:** As of 3 December 2025, the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* is Authorised Version No. 111, incorporating amendments as at 25 November 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (S.R. No. 3/2021) are in the version dated 25 November 2025 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

**What the law says about the situation**

- **The smoke alarm duty:** The landlord must ensure smoke alarms are working and tested at least once every 12 months, following the manufacturer's instructions [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Testing or repair of mains-powered alarms must be done by a suitably qualified person [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Entry rules:** For a purpose such as carrying out a duty under the Act, entry is allowed between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. on any day except a public holiday, with at least 24 hours' notice to the renter [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). This is my reading that a smoke alarm check falls under the "carry out a duty under this Act" purpose. The documents do not state this expressly [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Notice:** The notice must be in writing and state why the provider wants to enter. It must be delivered personally between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m., or sent by post [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Manner of entry:** The person entering must act reasonably and must not stay longer than needed without your consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

So a weekday is not a legal requirement. Entry can happen on any non-public-holiday day within those hours, provided the notice rules are met [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**Do you have to be home?** The documents do not say that you must personally be present. What they say is that you have a duty to permit a person exercising a right of entry to enter [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), and that you must allow entry where the provider has followed proper procedure [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Nothing I found says the renter must attend in person. I can't confirm whether you may arrange for someone else to let the inspector in.

**Can they charge $90?** The documents do not contain a rule that addresses a rebooking fee for a smoke alarm check during a tenancy. The closest provision, section 51(2), bars charging a fee for a renter's inspection of premises under a *proposed* agreement [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). That covers prospective renters, not an existing tenancy, so it does not answer your question. Section 51A deals with application and rent payment fees [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), which also doesn't fit. I can't say whether the $90 is lawful.

**What you can do or ask**

- **Agree a different time:** Entry can take place at any time agreed with you if you consented within 7 days before the entry [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). You can propose a time that suits you.
- **Check the notice:** Ask for written notice that states why entry is needed and gives at least 24 hours' notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Apply for limits:** You can apply to the Tribunal (VCAT) for an order specifying or limiting when entry may occur [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **If entry rules are broken:** You can apply to the Tribunal for an order stopping entry for a specified period [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), and for compensation if damage is caused to your goods during entry [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Ask for the fee's basis:** Request in writing the legal or contractual basis for the $90. The documents don't say whether such a fee is permitted.

The standard form says the rental provider must permit at least one fee-free payment method (other than the renter's own bank fees) and must allow Centrepay or another electronic transfer [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). A term requiring rent to be paid by a method that carries additional costs (other than bank or account fees) is a prohibited term [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Change of details:** The rental provider must notify the renter within 7 days if the provider or agent details change [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Contact-detail changes must be notified in writing immediately [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Receipts:** The renter is entitled to a receipt confirming rent payment [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Bond:** The provider or agent must lodge the bond with the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority (RTBA) within 10 business days of receiving it [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). If the renter has no RTBA receipt within 15 business days of paying, they may contact the RTBA [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). If the provider's rights and duties are transferred to another person, the provider and that person must notify the RTBA within 5 days, and the provider must give the renter a copy of that notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

**What to check before paying the new account**
1. **Written notice of the change** from the owner or agent, with the owner's full name and address for service, and contact details [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
2. **Payment method:** Confirm the new arrangement is a fee-free method (apart from your own bank fees), or Centrepay or electronic transfer [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
3. **Bond status:** Confirm your bond was lodged with the RTBA and that you have the bond lodgment form copy [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). If the owner is taking over the agreement, ask whether the RTBA notice under the transfer rules has been given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Receipts:** Make sure you will receive a receipt for each rent payment [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

**What you can ask for or do**
- Ask the agent or owner for the change in writing and the new provider details [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- Ask for confirmation that the new payment method carries no extra cost to you [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- If you have no RTBA receipt within 15 business days of paying the bond, contact the RTBA by email at rtba@justice.vic.gov.au [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The two forms list different RTBA phone numbers (1300 137 164 and 1300 13 71 64), so check the current number before calling [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

**Not covered by these documents:** How to verify that a bank account belongs to the owner, how to recognise payment fraud, and whether an owner can take over rent collection from an agent without a new agreement. If you're unsure, check with Consumer Affairs Victoria before transferring money.

- **Electronic payment facility charges are restricted.** A person must not demand or receive a charge for the establishment or use of direct debit facilities or "any other electronic payment facility for payment of rent". ## What the law says

- **Landlord's duty:** The landlord must keep the premises "in good repair" (s 68) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Cancelling before you move in:** A tenancy agreement terminates if you have not entered into possession and you give the landlord a notice of termination on the ground that the premises:
  - (a) "are not in good repair"
  - (b) "are unfit for human habitation"
  - (c) are destroyed or unsafe
  - (d) are not vacant
  - (e) are not legally available for use as a residence
  - (f) are "for any other reason unavailable for occupation" (s 226) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- **Vacant and clean on the agreed day:** The landlord must ensure the premises are vacant and reasonably clean on the agreed move-in day. You are not required to move in if they aren't, and you don't pay rent from the agreed day until you actually move in (s 65) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). This section covers vacancy and cleanliness. The retrieved text does not say that damp or rot falls under it.

## Your options

**1. Cancel (s 226).** Because you haven't moved in, you can give the landlord a notice of termination on the "not in good repair" ground. The "unfit for human habitation" or "unavailable for occupation" grounds may also fit [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Whether damp, mould and rotting timber meet any of these grounds depends on the facts, and the Act text doesn't settle that. The documents don't set out a required form or notice period for this notice. Don't move in before you give notice, because s 226 only applies if you haven't "entered into possession" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**2. Ask for repairs.**
- **Non-urgent repairs:** Give the landlord written notice. If the repairs aren't done within 14 days, you can apply to the Director to investigate (s 74) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
  - After the Director's report, you can apply to the Tribunal within 60 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
  - If you haven't received the report within 90 days, you can apply to the Tribunal without it (s 75) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
  - The Tribunal can order specified repairs and set a deadline (s 76) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs:** The list in this version includes a "serious roof leak" and "any fault or damage that makes rented premises… unsafe or insecure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Mould and damp are named as urgent only in the 2018 amendments, which are listed as not in operation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
  - If your problem does count as urgent, you may arrange the repairs yourself, but only after taking reasonable steps to get the landlord to do them and being unable to. You must give 14 days' written notice, and the landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost or $1000, whichever is less (s 72) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
  - You can also apply to the Tribunal for urgent repairs, and it must hear the application within 2 business days (s 73) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Rent into the Rent Special Account:** Once you have given notice requiring repairs, you can apply to the Tribunal for an order to pay rent into the Rent Special Account (s 77) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The Tribunal can make the order if the landlord has failed to do the repairs. This holds the rent but doesn't reduce it.

**3. Lower rent.** The retrieved text gives no direct right to cut the rent yourself for defects at the start of a tenancy.
- You may complain to the Director about excessive rent only where the landlord has reduced or withdrawn services or facilities, or after a rent-increase notice (s 45) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- If the Tribunal then considers the rent, it must take into account "the state of repair and general condition of the rented premises" (s 47(3)(b)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- The only rent relief for the period before you move in is under s 65(3), and it applies to premises that aren't vacant or reasonably clean [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

## What the law said on 15 October 2019

The applicable law was the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic), Authorised Version No. 088, incorporating amendments as at 2 July 2019**. That version was in force on 15 October 2019. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

The rental provider had to ensure that the premises were **in good repair** and in a **reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation**, regardless of whether the renter knew about the disrepair before entering into occupation. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) Damp, mould and rotting timber may therefore amount to a breach, depending on their extent and effect, but the retrieved documents do not define exactly when those particular defects make premises “unfit for human habitation.” [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

The Act also contained a specific rule allowing a tenant to terminate before possession where the premises were, among other things, **not in good repair, unfit for human habitation, unsafe, or otherwise unavailable for occupation**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) The retrieved extract does not include the section number or full operative wording of that provision, so I cannot state the required notice procedure more precisely from these documents.

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask to cancel/terminate immediately.**  
   Write to the rental provider or agent, describe the damp, mould and rotten timber, attach photographs or reports, and say you seek termination because the premises are not in good repair and/or are unfit for occupation. The Act provides a termination route for premises in those conditions. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

2. **Ask for repairs.**  
   The rental provider must arrange for the premises to be put and kept in good repair and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) For non-urgent repairs, give written notice. If the repairs are not done within **14 days**, you may apply to the Director for an investigation; you may then apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring specified repairs if satisfactory arrangements have not been made. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

3. **Do not move in while the premises are unsuitable.**  
   The law expressly says a tenant is not required to enter into occupation of premises that do not meet the statutory provision about being vacant and reasonably clean. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) However, the retrieved documents do not clearly state whether simply collecting the keys counts as “entering into possession” for the termination-before-possession provision.

4. **Ask for lower rent, but the documents do not establish an automatic right to a rent reduction.**  
   You can ask the rental provider to agree to a lower rent if you are willing to accept the premises after repairs or with reduced amenity. The retrieved provisions instead provide for repair orders, compensation in an appropriate Tribunal proceeding, and—after notice of required repairs—an application to pay rent into the **Rent Special Account**; they do not state a general right to unilaterally reduce the agreed rent. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

5. **Do not simply stop paying rent without an order or agreement.**  
   The Act provides a specific Tribunal process for paying rent into the Rent Special Account where repairs have been notified and the rental provider has failed to comply. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

Keep the keys, lease, inspection/condition report, photographs, messages and any building or health report. The retrieved documents do not say whether you can recover the bond or moving-related costs on these facts.

Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic)**, Authorised Version No. 088, which was in force on 15 October 2019 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf), here are your options regarding the damp, mould, and rotting timber you found before moving in:

### 🔑 Can you cancel or refuse to move in?
The Act does not use the word "cancel" for this scenario, but it gives you a clear right to refuse entry. Under section 65(1), your landlord must ensure the premises are vacant and in a reasonably clean condition on the agreed occupation day [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). If the property has damp, mould, or rotting timber, it likely fails this standard. 

Section 65(2) explicitly states that you are **not required to enter into occupation** of premises that do not comply with this duty [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Furthermore, if you choose not to move in, section 65(3) protects you from paying rent for the period between the agreed start date and the day you actually enter (if you eventually do) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

### 🛠️ Can you ask for repairs?
Yes. Section 68(1) places a strict duty on your landlord to ensure the rented premises are maintained in good repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). You should formally notify your landlord or agent of the defects in writing. Depending on the severity, you have two main pathways:
* **Urgent Repairs:** If the damp/mould poses an immediate health or safety risk (e.g., structural rotting timber), it may qualify as an urgent repair. You can apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring the landlord to fix it, and the Tribunal must hear your application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
* **Non-Urgent Repairs:** If it is not immediately dangerous, you can apply to the Director of Housing to investigate whether the landlord is breaching their repair duty. If the issue remains unresolved after 14 days from your notice, and the Director's report doesn't satisfy you, you can then apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring the repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

### 💰 Can you ask for lower rent?
The Act does not allow tenants to unilaterally reduce their rent. However, if the landlord fails to carry out required repairs after you have given proper notice, section 77 allows you to apply to the Tribunal for an order to pay your rent into a **Rent Special Account** (escrow) instead of paying the landlord directly [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The Tribunal will only authorise this if satisfied that a repair notice has been given and the landlord has failed to comply with their duty [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

### 📝 Recommended Next Steps
1. Document the damp, mould, and rotting timber with photos/videos immediately.
2. Send a written notice to your landlord/agent citing section 65(1) (condition on occupation day) and section 68(1) (duty to maintain in good repair), stating you will not take possession until the issues are resolved.
3. If they refuse or delay, contact the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) or Consumer Affairs Victoria for guidance on filing an application under sections 73–75 or 77 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

To pay into a new bank account, both you and the owner must agree to change the payment method under your residential rental agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). 
* **Payment Costs:** The owner or their agent must ensure that a payment method with no additional costs (other than standard bank fees) is reasonably available to you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). * **Receipts:** Anyone receiving your rent must give you a written receipt. If you pay in person, it must be given immediately; if you pay electronically and request a receipt at the time, it must be provided within 5 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

**Short answer:** Under the law in force on 15 January 2026, the app most likely cannot charge you a card fee for paying rent. The documents don't expressly say that a card surcharge is covered, so that conclusion is my reading of the wording. Who receives the fee doesn't change the answer, because the prohibition applies to any person who demands or receives the charge [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**What the law says**

- **Version applied:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, version 111 (file rta-1997-v111-2025-11-25.pdf), in force from 25 November 2025 to 29 June 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The regulations version in force is *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, version 005, in force until 9 February 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- **Card fees (s 51(3)(b)):** A person must not demand or receive from a renter a charge or indemnity for a charge relating to "the establishment or use of direct debit facilities or any other electronic payment facility for payment of rent." The penalty is 60 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). This is the provision most relevant to a card surcharge, though the documents don't say whether a card fee counts as a charge for "use" of an electronic payment facility.
- **Fee-free method (s 42(4)):** The provider or agent must ensure that a payment method incurring no additional costs (other than the renter's bank or account fees) is reasonably available. The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person or 400 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). A manual bank transfer with no fee fits this description, as you describe it. The documents say nothing about speed, so slowness isn't a legal reason to refuse it.
- **Cost disclosure (s 42(7)):** Before you consent to a payment method, the provider or agent must tell you about costs you may incur, including third-party transaction fees and other electronic payment facility fees [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Electronic transfer (s 42(5) and reg 19):** Providers must permit Centrepay and any prescribed payment method. Regulation 19 prescribes electronic funds transfer [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The documents don't clearly say whether a manual bank transfer is an electronic funds transfer, so you should not rely on this point alone.
- **Application and rent payment fees (s 51A):** The version 111 text prohibits fees for prescribed matters, including rent payment "other than payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). However, the list of prescribed matters is in regulation 21C, which "has effect on and after 31 March 2026" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). So this prohibition does not appear to apply yet on 15 January 2026.

**Does it matter who gets the fee?**

Not under s 51(3)(b), which applies to anyone who demands or receives the charge [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Under s 42(4), the duty to provide a no-cost method falls on the provider or agent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The documents don't address whether an app company that is not the agent is bound by s 42. The s 51A rule that would reach a business such as an app company does not yet apply, as noted above [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask**

1. Ask the agent in writing what each payment method costs, since they must tell you before you consent to a method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
2. Confirm in writing that the fee-free bank transfer is available, since s 42(4) requires it to be reasonably available [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
3. You are not required to accept a fee-bearing card method as the only option. The documents don't say you must consent to any particular method.
4. If you pay by bank transfer and want a receipt, you can request one at the time of payment. For a payment not made in person, the receipt must be given within 5 business days of receiving the payment [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't say what remedies apply if the app charges a fee anyway, or which body to complain to. I can't answer that from these sources.

The documents include *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* version 009 (in force from 30 June 2026) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) and *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* version 115 (in force from 13 October 2026) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Neither was in force on 15 January 2026, so I haven't relied on them.

I applied the law in force on 3 December 2025: the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* Authorised Version No. 111 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* Authorised Version No. 005 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). ### What the law says

- **Smoke alarm duty:** The provider must ensure any smoke alarm is "correctly installed and in working condition," has batteries, and is "tested at least once every 12 months in accordance with any instructions by the manufacturer of the smoke alarm" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The provider or agent must "immediately arrange for the repairs to be carried out" if an alarm doesn't meet these requirements [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Entry for this purpose:** The provider may enter "to do an inspection but not more than once every 12 months" and "to comply with the rental provider's duties under the Act" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). A smoke alarm test falls under those duties [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Duty to allow entry:** "The renter must allow entry to the premises where the rental provider has followed proper procedure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

### Do you have to be there?

The retrieved documents don't say whether a renter must be personally present. The Act's entry provisions (the notice and manner-of-entry rules) aren't in the in-force excerpts I retrieved, so I can't confirm the rule. Your obligation is to allow entry where proper procedure has been followed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

### Can they charge $90?

No retrieved document mentions a rebooking fee for inspections, so I can't say it's lawful or unlawful. The smoke alarm duty is placed on the provider [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), and nothing I found shifts the cost of the check to the renter.

### What you can do or ask

- **Check the 12-month limit.** If an entry for an inspection has already happened in the past 12 months, the provider's right to inspect for that purpose may not apply [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Note that one excerpt labelled Authorised Version 005 gives a 6-month limit for the same provision, so check the authorised text before relying on either figure.
- **Ask for the basis in writing.** Ask the agent which duty requires entry, what the fee is based on, and where it is authorised.
- **Offer other times.** The provider may enter "at any time, if the renter has agreed within the last 7 days" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). You can agree to a different time, but the documents don't say the provider must accept a set window.
- **Get help.** The Regulations list Consumer Affairs Victoria on 1300 55 81 81 for contract questions [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

### What the documents don't cover

- Whether you must be personally present.
- The notice period and delivery rules for entry under the in-force Act.
- Whether a rebooking fee can be charged for a smoke alarm check.

The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person and 400 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The standard rental agreement form repeats this: the provider must permit a fee-free payment method other than the renter's own bank fees [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- **Charges for electronic payment facilities.** A person must not demand or receive from a renter a charge for "the establishment or use of direct debit facilities or any other electronic payment facility for payment of rent" (s 51(3)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The penalty is 60 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). This applies to "a person", and the text doesn't limit it to the provider or agent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). A card payment through a rent app could be an "electronic payment facility", but the retrieved text doesn't say so.
- **Fees to third parties.** A person carrying on a business must not demand or receive a fee for any *prescribed matter* relating to the payment of rent (s 51A) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The provider, the provider's agent and authorised deposit-taking institutions (such as banks) are excluded from this rule [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Cost disclosure.** The provider or agent must tell you about any costs you may incur by using a payment method, including third party transaction fees and other electronic payment facility fees, before you consent to that method (s 42(7)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

## Does it matter who gets the fee?

It may, but the documents don't resolve it.

- **Section 51(3)** refers to "a person", so it does not turn on whether the fee goes to the app company or the agent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Section 51A** does turn on who charges. In version 111 it excludes providers and agents, so it would only reach a separate app company, and only for a "prescribed matter" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The retrieved documents don't list the prescribed matters, so I can't say whether a card fee is one.
- A later version, "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf" (version 115, from 13 October 2026), words s 51A differently. It excludes only authorised deposit-taking institutions [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). That version was not in force on 15 January 2026, so it doesn't apply to your question.

## What you can do

1. **Use the free bank transfer.** Section 42(4) is about a no-cost method being "reasonably available" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The documents don't define "reasonably available" or say whether a slower method meets it.
2. **Ask for the fee in writing.** The agent must disclose any card or transaction fee before you consent to that method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
3. **Ask the agent to confirm** which payment method is the fee-free one under your agreement, and whether the card fee is charged by the app or by the agency. The standard form requires a fee-free method to be permitted [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
4. **Check your agreement.** Rent is payable in the manner specified in the agreement. You and the provider can change that only by agreement (s 42(2), (6)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

If you want a firm answer on whether the card fee is unlawful, the retrieved documents don't provide one. You would need the regulation that prescribes the matters under s 51A, or advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy advice service.

# Changing the rent account: what to check (as at 8 November 2022)

**Sources used:** the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v101-2022-09-07.pdf", version 101. It was in force from 7 September 2022 to 23 May 2023, so it covers your date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). I also used the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, file "rt-regs-2021-v002-2022-06-01.pdf", version 002, in force from 1 June 2022 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The retrieved text doesn't show the formal "Authorised Version No." line, so the version numbers come from the file labels and metadata. I did not use the later versions (v110, v111, v115), because they were not in force on your date.

## What the law says

- **Where and how rent is paid:** Rent is payable in the manner specified in your agreement. If the agreement names a place, rent is paid there. If it names none, rent is paid at the rented premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf) (s 42(1)–(2)).
- **Changing the payment method needs your agreement:** The rental provider and the renter "by agreement" may change how rent is payable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf) (s 42(6)). The documents don't say the owner can change it alone.
- **Fee-free option:** The rental provider or their agent must make sure a payment method with no extra costs (other than your own bank fees) is reasonably available to you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf) (s 42(4)). They must also let you pay by Centrepay or any prescribed method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf) (s 42(5)).
- **Fee information:** Before you agree to a payment method, you must be told about any costs you might incur, such as third-party transaction fees or direct debit dishonour fees [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf) (s 42(7)).
- **Receipts:**
  - If you pay in person, you must get a written receipt immediately.
  - If you pay another way, you must get a receipt within 5 business days of the payment, if you ask for it when you pay [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf) (s 43(1)).
  - A receipt must be signed by the person who receives the payment. It must state your name and the premises, the date, the period paid for, the amount, and that it is for rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf) (s 43(3)).
  - If no receipt is required, the recipient must keep a record for up to 12 months. They must give you a copy within 5 business days of your request [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf) (s 43(2), (2A)).
- **Change of agent or provider details:** The prescribed rental agreement form records the agent's details and the provider's details. It says the rental provider must notify the renter within 7 days if any of that information changes [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf) (Form 1, item 3). The form also lists the provider's preferred payment methods and payment details, and says you are entitled to a receipt [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf) (Form 1, item 8).

## What you can do or ask

1. **Compare with your lease.** Check the payment details and methods in the lease (Form 1, item 8, if you're on the prescribed form) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Anything different is a change that needs your agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask for written notice of the change.** The form requires the provider to notify you within 7 days of changes to the provider's or agent's details [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Ask for the owner's name and contact details in writing.
3. **Ask the owner to confirm the new account, and ask for a receipt.** Do this through the agency or another contact you already trust. You can request a receipt when you pay, and it is due within 5 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Check for fees and a fee-free option.** Ask about any costs of the new method and for a no-cost option [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
5. **Keep proof of payment** and the receipt or record.

## What the documents don't cover

- The retrieved text has no rule on how a change of agent or owner must be verified, or on how bank details can be changed. Checking the new account by calling the agency or owner on a number you already hold is common-sense fraud protection, not a requirement from these documents.
- The bond: the form says the bond must be lodged with the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority within 10 business days of payment. It also says that if you have no receipt within 15 business days of paying, you can email rtba@justice.vic.gov.au or call the RTBA on 1300 137 164 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf) (Form 1, item 7). I haven't verified this against any other document, and Form 2 gives a different phone number [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf), so check the number before you call.

## What the law says — 15 January 2026

On that date, the applicable Act was the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 111, in force from 25 November 2025**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) The applicable regulations were the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 005, in force from 25 November 2025**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

The rental provider or agent **must ensure that a rent-payment method with no additional cost**—apart from bank or account fees on your own bank account—is **reasonably available** to you. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) Therefore, the app may charge a card-payment fee **only if** the no-fee bank-transfer option is reasonably available. The fact that the transfer is slower is not addressed in the retrieved documents, so they do not say whether that makes it unreasonable.

Before you consent to use a payment method, the rental provider or agent must tell you about costs you may incur, including **third-party transaction fees** and **other electronic payment facility fees**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) The documents do not say that the result changes depending on whether the fee is retained by the app company or paid to the agent. They also do not expressly state who is legally entitled to receive such a fee.

The prescribed rental agreement form confirms that at least one payment method must be fee-free, apart from the renter’s own bank fees, and refers to bank deposit or another electronic funds transfer as available payment options. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

- Ask the agent or rental provider to confirm in writing that the bank-transfer option is the required **fee-free payment method** and that it is reasonably available. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- Ask for the card fee and any other payment-method costs to be disclosed in writing before using the card option. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- Ask whether the fee is a third-party transaction fee or electronic payment facility fee, and who receives it. The documents require cost information but do not provide a rule answering the recipient question. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- If the transfer option is not reasonably available in practice, the retrieved documents do not provide a specific procedure or test for resolving that issue.

### What the law says
*   **Right to a fee-free method:** The landlord or their agent must ensure that a rent payment method that incurs **no additional costs** (other than your own bank's standard account fees) is reasonably available to you at all times [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

*   **Regulatory confirmation:** The standard tenancy agreement explicitly notes that providers must permit a fee-free payment method and allow the use of Centrepay or other electronic funds transfers [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

### Can the app charge you the card fee?
Yes, but only under strict conditions:
1.  **You cannot be forced to pay it.** Because your landlord/agent has already provided a manual bank transfer option with no fee, they are legally meeting their obligation to provide a reasonably available fee-free method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

No, it does not change your legal rights:
*   The law focuses on the **cost incurred by you** (categorized as "third party transaction fees" or "electronic payment facility fees") rather than who pockets the money [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

*   *Practical distinction:* If the agent is illegally demanding you pay a card fee while denying you the free option, the breach falls on the landlord/agent under the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). If the app charges a standard processing fee for a service you voluntarily selected, that is a separate commercial arrangement between you and the app provider.

### What you can do
*   **Use the free option:** Simply pay via the manual bank transfer to avoid the fee entirely.
*   **Report non-compliance:** If your landlord or agent pressures you into using card payments or refuses to accept the fee-free bank transfer, they are breaching their legal obligations [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). - **If the app company keeps it:** The app is not one of the people exempt under section 51A(2) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), so the app's fee falls under the section 51A ban once a prescribed matter covers it, which is from 31 March 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- **If the agent takes it:** Agents are exempt from section 51A(1) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). However, the agent still must make a fee-free method available [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) and must disclose costs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The penalty for breaching that duty is the same whoever receives the money.

The documents don't define "payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act," so I can't say which surcharges are permitted.

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Ask for the bank transfer option in writing.** It is fee-free apart from your own bank fees, so it appears to satisfy the requirement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The documents don't address whether a slower method is "reasonably available," so that point is unresolved.
2. **Ask for the cost details before you choose a payment method.** The landlord or agent must give this information before you consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
3. **Ask for a receipt.** If you request one when paying electronically, it must be provided within 5 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
4. **Ask whether the lease permits a method change.** Payment method can be changed by agreement between you and the landlord [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't cover dispute procedures or how to enforce these rules, so please check with Consumer Affairs Victoria or VCAT before taking formal action.

**Short answer:** Under the version of the Act in force on 15 October 2019, you can likely give notice to end the lease, arrange urgent repairs or seek a repair order, and in some cases withhold rent. The documents do not give a clear right to a rent reduction for these defects.

**Governing law:** The *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (No. 109 of 1997), Authorised Version No. 088, incorporating amendments as at 2 July 2019, applies on your date. It was in force from 2 July 2019 to 3 December 2019 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The document also contains amendment text in its endnotes that uses "residential rental provider" and "renter" terms, but it does not say when that text commences. I have relied on the body of the Act. The Act states that references to landlords and tenants are read as references to residential rental providers and renters [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

### What the law says

- **Repairs duty:** A landlord must ensure rented premises are maintained in good repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Condition at move-in:** A landlord must ensure that, on the agreed day you enter occupation, the premises are vacant and reasonably clean. You are not required to move into premises that do not comply, and you need not pay rent for the period before you actually move in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Condition report:** If you pay a bond, the landlord must give you two copies of a condition report before you enter occupation, specifying the state of repair. You must return a signed copy within 3 business days of moving in, and you can endorse that you disagree with any part of it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). A signed report is conclusive evidence of state of repair, unless the defect could not reasonably have been discovered on inspection or you disagree with it under an endorsement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

### Your options

**1. Cancel (end the agreement)**
- If you have not entered into possession, the tenancy terminates if you give the landlord a notice of termination on the ground that the premises "are not in good repair" or "are unfit for human habitation" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- If you have moved in, you may give a notice of intention to vacate if the premises are unfit for human habitation. The termination date may be the date the notice is given or a later date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- The documents do not define "entered into possession," so it is unclear whether picking up the keys counts. Take advice on this point.

**2. Ask for repairs**
- **Notify in writing:** You must give the landlord written notice of non-urgent repairs. If they are not carried out within 14 days, you can apply to the Director to investigate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs:** You may arrange urgent repairs if you have taken reasonable steps to get the landlord to do them immediately and they cannot or will not. You must give the landlord 14 days' written notice of the repairs and cost. The landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost or $1000, whichever is less [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repair definition:** Urgent repairs include any fault or damage that makes the premises unsafe or insecure [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The body text does not expressly list damp or mould. The endnote amendment that adds "presence of mould or damp" is not confirmed as in force by the documents [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Tribunal:** You may apply to VCAT (the Tribunal) for an order requiring specified repairs. For non-urgent repairs, you must apply within 60 days of receiving the Director's report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). For urgent repairs, the Tribunal must hear the application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**3. Ask for lower rent**
- The documents do not contain a general right to reduce rent for initial defects.
- The closest provision is the excessive rent process. The Tribunal must declare rent excessive if it is more than a tenant should reasonably pay, having regard to, among other things, the "state of repair and general condition of the rented premises" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). This process is framed around rent increases and reduced services, so its application to a new lease is uncertain [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- If you have given a repair notice and the landlord has failed to comply, you may apply to the Tribunal to pay rent into the Rent Special Account [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). This is a pressure tool, not a reduction.
- Rent is not payable for any period before you actually move in if the premises do not comply with the move-in duty [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

### Practical steps

1. Put your complaint in writing now, listing the damp, mould and rotting timber.
2. Check the condition report, if one has been given. Endorse any disagreement within 3 business days of moving in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
3. Photograph everything.
4. Keep records of all communication and costs.

**Not covered by the documents:** The documents do not cover whether the lease can be cancelled without other consequences, or whether a rent reduction is available for initial defects. This is general information based only on the retrieved text, not legal advice. Consider speaking to Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy legal service.

**What the law says**

Under the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Version 111, in force from 25 November 2025) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), the provider must ensure every smoke alarm is correctly installed and working, has batteries, and is tested at least once every 12 months [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The provider can enter to carry out that duty [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The entry rules are:

- **Hours:** Entry is allowed at any time agreed with the renter if the renter consented within the previous 7 days. Otherwise, entry is allowed between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. on any day except a public holiday, with at least 24 hours' notice [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Notice:** The notice must be in writing, state why the provider wants to enter, and be given by post or delivered personally between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Manner:** The provider must enter in a reasonable manner and must not stay longer than necessary without your consent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Your duty:** A renter must permit entry that complies with the Act [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The Regulations (Version 005, in force from 25 November 2025) say the renter must allow entry where the provider has followed proper procedure [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

**Do you have to be there yourself?**

The retrieved documents do not say whether you must be personally present. They only set out the hours, notice and manner rules above, and your duty to allow entry that follows them [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). I can't confirm from these sources whether you have to be home.

**Can they charge you $90?**

The documents do not cover this. Nothing I retrieved addresses a rebooking fee for a missed or rescheduled inspection. The only fee provisions I found are about consent to assignment or sub-letting [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) and rental application and rent payment fees, which only take effect on 31 March 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Neither applies here, so I can't say whether the $90 fee is lawful.

**Points to raise with your agent**

- The Act allows entry between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. on non-public-holiday days, so the 10 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. window is narrower than the statute [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). A different time may still be agreed with you [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- Ask for the entry notice in writing, stating the reason for entry, with at least 24 hours' notice, and delivered in the way the Act requires [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- Ask the agent to put the $90 charge in writing and identify the provision that authorises it. If you disagree, you can check guidance at the Consumer Affairs Victoria renting website, which the Regulations refer to [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). You can also ask VCAT for an order limiting when entry may occur [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**Short answer:** The documents don't say how to verify a bank account, and they don't address payment fraud. They do set out rules on how rent may be paid and changed, and on the bond and receipts, which you can check before paying.

**What the law says**

- Where the rent is payable depends on the agreement. Rent is payable at the place the agreement specifies, or at the premises if none is specified, and otherwise in the manner the agreement specifies [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- The manner of payment can change only by agreement. The rental provider and renter, "by agreement, may change the manner in which rent is payable" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). So a unilateral notice of new bank details is not, on the text, a change you're bound by.
- Before you agree to a payment method, the provider or agent must tell you about any costs you may incur by using it, such as third-party transaction fees [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- The provider or agent must make a no-extra-cost payment method reasonably available, other than your own bank or account fees [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). They must also permit payment by Centrepay [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- If the new owner or agent changes, the standard lease form requires the rental provider to notify the renter within 7 days if agent details change [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- Any payment you make must be receipted. For a payment not made in person, a receipt must be given within 5 business days if you request one. The receipt must be signed and state your name and the premises, the date, the period paid for, the amount, and that it is for rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

**What to check and ask before paying**

1. **Ask for the change in writing and confirm the payment method is agreed.** Because changing the payment manner requires agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf), you can decline to pay into a new account until you have agreed to the change.
2. **Ask about fees.** Ask whether any fees apply to the new account or method, since the provider must give you that information before you consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
3. **Confirm who the landlord and agent are.** The lease form requires notice within 7 days of changes to agent details [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Check that the person sending the new details is the owner named on your agreement or an authorised agent. An agent must produce evidence of their authorisation if the Bond Authority asks [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Check the bond.** The provider or agent must lodge the bond with the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority (RTBA) within 10 business days of receiving it. The RTBA sends a receipt. If you have not received one within 15 business days of paying, you may email rtba@justice.vic.gov.au or call 1300 137 164 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Confirm the bond is lodged before the handover.
5. **Keep records.** Keep receipts for every rent payment [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover**

- They don't say whether a switch from an agency to owner-management counts as a transfer of the landlord's rights. If it does, the owner must notify the Bond Authority within 5 days and give you a copy of the notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether that applies here, so you may wish to ask.
- They don't set out how to verify a bank account, and they don't address scams. Confirming the new details with the owner or agent through contact information you already have is a practical step, but it is my suggestion, not something the documents require.

**Sources**
