answer:
## What the law says

**Documents used:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v111-2025-11-25.pdf" (dated 25 Nov 2025, version 111, in force 25 Nov 2025 to 29 Jun 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). I also used the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, file "rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf" (dated 25 Nov 2025, version 005, in force to 9 Feb 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Both were in force on 15 January 2026. I'm taking the version numbers from the documents' metadata. The retrieved text doesn't show an "Authorised Version" label.

**1. A fee-free option must be reasonably available (s 42(4)).**
- The rental provider or their agent must ensure a rent payment method that incurs no additional costs, other than fees on your own bank account, is reasonably available to you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person and 400 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- The standard-form agreement repeats this. The provider must permit a fee-free payment method other than the renter's own bank fees [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- Your free bank transfer therefore appears to meet this duty. The documents don't define "reasonably available", so they don't say whether "slower" changes that.

**2. Fees must be disclosed first (s 42(7)).**
- The provider or agent must tell you about any costs you may incur by using a payment method before you consent to it. This expressly includes third-party transaction fees and other electronic payment facility fees [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- That wording shows the Act contemplates that some payment methods carry fees.

**3. Some charges are banned outright (s 51(3)).**
- A person must not demand or receive from a renter a charge for the first issue of a rent payment card [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- A person must not demand or receive a charge for "the establishment or use of direct debit facilities or any other electronic payment facility for payment of rent". The penalty is 60 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- The documents don't say whether a card-payment surcharge counts as a charge for using an "electronic payment facility". I can't give you a definite yes or no on that.

## Does it matter who gets the fee?

It may, but the documents only partly answer this.

- **Fee to the agent or rental provider:** The s 42(4) duty applies to them, as does s 42(7) disclosure [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Section 51(3) applies to "a person", so it isn't limited to who receives the money [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Fee to a separate app company:**
  - Section 51A bars a business, other than the provider, the provider's agent or a bank-type deposit-taking institution, from demanding or receiving a fee for "any prescribed matter" relating to rent payment [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person and 400 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

The retrieved documents don't cover how to make a complaint or enforce these rules, so I can't advise on that.

answer:
**Document used:** *rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf*, the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 088, which incorporates amendments as at 2 July 2019 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Its metadata shows it was in force from 2 July 2019 to 3 December 2019, so it covers 15 October 2019 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- The landlord must keep the rented premises "in good repair" (s 68) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- Two provisions do apply to premises that are not in a fit state before you move in:
  - If the premises are not in good repair, are unfit for human habitation, or are unavailable for occupation for any other reason, the tenancy ends if you have not yet entered into possession and you give the landlord a notice of termination on that ground (s 226) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
  - Section 226 lists those grounds as (a) not in good repair, (b) unfit for human habitation, and (f) unavailable for occupation for any other reason [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- Some newer amendments are not in operation in this version. They include adding "mould or damp" to urgent repairs, adding a "rental minimum standards" ground to the pre-possession termination provision, and the change from "tenant" to "renter" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The document lists the amending provisions as "Not in Operation" at its publication date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). I have therefore relied on the main text only.

## Your options

**1. Cancel the lease before moving in**
- You can give the landlord a notice of termination under s 226, on the grounds that the premises are not in good repair, are unfit for habitation, or are unavailable for occupation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- This only works if you have "not entered into possession" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether collecting the keys counts as entering into possession. Don't move in or move belongings in until you've resolved this.

**2. Ask for repairs**
- *Urgent repairs:*
  - The definition includes a "serious roof leak" and "any fault or damage that makes rented premises… unsafe or insecure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Damp, mould and rotting timber aren't named in the in-force definition, so whether yours qualifies depends on how serious the fault is.
  - If it qualifies, you may arrange the repairs yourself, but only after taking reasonable steps to get the landlord or agent to do them immediately and being unable to [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
  - You must give the landlord 14 days' written notice of the repairs and their cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
  - The landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost or $1000, whichever is less [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
  - You can also apply to VCAT for an order for urgent repairs, and the Tribunal must hear it within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- *Non-urgent repairs:*
  - Give the landlord written notice. If the repairs aren't done within 14 days, you can apply in writing to the Director to investigate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
  - You can then apply to the Tribunal within 60 days of receiving the Director's report. You can also apply if you haven't received the report within 90 days of asking for it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
  - If the Tribunal finds a breach of the duty to maintain, it may order specified repairs and must set a deadline [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- *Rent into the Rent Special Account:* once you've given notice requiring repairs, you can ask the Tribunal to let you pay rent into the Rent Special Account. The Tribunal may order this if the landlord has failed to do the repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**3. Ask for lower rent**
- The documents give no automatic right to reduce rent yourself because of defects.
- A duty-breach route may lead to a rent reduction:
  - Section 68 is a "duty provision" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
  - You can give a breach of duty notice, which must specify the breach, the loss, and require the landlord to remedy or compensate within the required time. For these duties that is 14 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
  - If the landlord doesn't comply, you can apply to the Tribunal for a compensation or compliance order [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
  - The Tribunal can order the breach remedied, compensation paid, or the landlord to refrain from repeating it. Compensation may take the form of "a refund or reduction of the rent" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- The "excessive rent" complaint to the Director applies where the landlord has reduced services or where you've received a rent increase notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). It doesn't clearly fit your situation. If it did apply, the Tribunal considers "the state of repair and general condition" of the premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

## Practical point

Record the defects in the condition report. A signed condition report is conclusive evidence of the premises' condition, unless it was endorsed with your disagreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). You must return your copy within 3 business days after entering occupation, signed or endorsed as agreeing or disagreeing [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

## Not covered

The documents don't say whether collecting keys means you've "entered into possession". They don't set a notice period for a s 226 termination. They also don't say whether damp, mould and rotting timber is "unfit for human habitation" in your case.

## What the law says

I used the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 111** (incorporating amendments as at 25 November 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Its metadata shows it was in force from 25 Nov 2025 to 29 Jun 2026, so it applies on 3 December 2025. I also used the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021** (file `rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf`, version 005, in force 25 Nov 2025 to 9 Feb 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The regulations text I retrieved doesn't show an "Authorised Version No." label, so that version number comes from the file metadata.

**Do you have to be home?**
- A rental provider must test smoke alarms at least once every 12 months [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Mains-powered alarms must be tested by a suitably qualified person [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- An agent may enter between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. on any day except a public holiday. For entry to carry out the provider's duty under the Act, that needs at least 24 hours' notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). A smoke alarm check fits this ground, though that is my inference. The documents don't name smoke alarm checks as an entry purpose.
- The notice must be in writing, say why they want to enter, and be given by post or delivered personally between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- Alternatively, they can enter at a time you agreed, if you consented within the 7 days before entry [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- You have a duty to *permit* entry that is made in accordance with these rules [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The documents I retrieved do not say you must be present. They only require that you not obstruct a lawful entry. I can't say from them whether the agent can insist you stay home.
- Entry must be in a reasonable manner, and they can't stay longer than necessary without your consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**Can they charge $90?**
- The documents contain no provision allowing a "rebooking fee" for a smoke alarm check.
- A person must not demand or accept from a renter who has failed to comply with the agreement or Act any amount other than rent or an amount provided for in the Act. The penalty is 150 penalty units for a natural person and 750 for a body corporate [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- A lease term that imposes fees for safety-related maintenance that is the rental provider's responsibility is a prescribed prohibited term [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). A prohibited term is void and unenforceable [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Smoke alarm testing is the provider's duty, so this probably covers the fee. That is my reading, and the regulations don't mention smoke alarms in that provision.
- I can't tell from the documents whether your lease contains this fee.

## What you can do

- **Ask for the written notice.** Check that it gives at least 24 hours' notice, states the reason, and falls between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Propose a time.** The Act lets you and the agent agree a time, as long as you consent within 7 days before entry [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Ask the agent which section or lease term authorises the $90 fee.** I found none. Refuse to pay it, and refer to the provisions above [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- **Apply to the Tribunal.** You can apply for an order limiting the days and times of entry [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). If an agent exercises entry without following the rules, you can apply for an order restraining entry for a set period [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Report improper entry.** An agent who enters other than in accordance with these rules, without reasonable excuse, commits an offence carrying 60 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

I'd avoid blocking a properly notified entry. Failing to permit it can be treated as a breach of your duty under the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**Documents used:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (file rta-1997-v101-2022-09-07.pdf, version 101, dated 7 September 2022, in force 7 Sept 2022 to 23 May 2023) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). Both were in force on 8 November 2022. The excerpts I retrieved show the version number only in the file metadata, not as a printed "Authorised Version No." line.

## What the law says

- **Where and how rent is paid:** Rent is payable at the place specified in the agreement, or at the premises if none is specified. It is payable in the manner specified in the agreement [1, s 42(1)–(2)]. The provider and renter may change the manner of payment *by agreement* [1, s 42(6)].
- **No-cost and electronic payment:** The provider or their agent must make a payment method with no extra cost (other than your own bank fees) reasonably available. They must also permit payment by Centrepay and any prescribed method [1, s 42(4)–(5)]. The prescribed method is electronic funds transfer [2, reg 19]. They must tell you about any fees before you consent to a payment method [1, s 42(7)].
- **Change of agent or provider details:** If there is no agent, the provider must give you their full name, an address for service of documents and an emergency phone number. If there is an agent, they must give the agent's details instead [1, s 66(2)–(3)]. The provider must tell you in writing of any change in that information within 7 days after the change [1, s 66(4)]. The standard agreement form also records the provider's and agent's details and notes the 7-day duty to notify changes [2, Form 1, item 3].
- **Receipts:** Anyone who receives rent must give a written receipt. If you pay by transfer and ask for a receipt when you pay, it is due within 5 business days. The receipt must be signed and state your name and the premises, the date, the period paid for, the amount, and that it is for rent [1, s 43(1), (3)]. If no receipt is required, the recipient must keep a record for 12 months. If you ask for a copy, they must give it within 5 business days [1, s 43(2), (2A)].

## What you can check or ask

1. **Ask for the change in writing.** The Act requires written notice of a change in who is acting (owner instead of agent) [1, s 66(4)]. Ask for the owner's full name, address for service and emergency number [1, s 66(2)].
2. **Compare the details with your lease.** Check the "payment details" and provider/agent details in your agreement [2, Form 1, items 3 and 8]. A different bank account is a change in the manner of payment, which the Act says is done by agreement [1, s 42(6)]. You can ask for the change to be agreed in writing.
3. **Check there is no extra cost.** Confirm that a no-cost method, including electronic transfer, remains available [1, s 42(4)–(5); 2, reg 19], and ask about any fees [1, s 42(7)].
4. **Ask for receipts.** Request a receipt when you pay, so the owner has to issue one that meets the s 43(3) requirements [1, s 43(1), (3)].
5. **Check your bond receipt.** The standard form says the bond must be lodged with the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority within 10 business days of payment, and the Authority sends you a receipt. If you have none within 15 business days of paying, you can email rtba@justice.vic.gov.au or call the Authority [2, Form 1, item 7]. The number printed there is 1300 137 164 in Form 1 and 1300 13 71 64 in Form 2, so check which is correct.

**Not covered:** The retrieved documents don't say whether an unverified change of bank account is valid, or how to verify that the new account belongs to the owner. They also don't say what happens if you pay into a wrong account. To confirm the change independently, use the contact details in your signed agreement, not only those in the new message.

**Timing:** These provisions apply to agreements made after the 2018 amendments. The Act has transitional rules for older tenancies [1, Sch 1, cl 16]. A recently signed lease should not be affected.

## What the law says

On **15 January 2026**, the applicable documents are:

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 111, dated 25 November 2025** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 005, dated 25 November 2025** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

The rental provider or agent **must ensure that a rent-payment method with no additional cost**—apart from bank or account fees payable on your own bank account—is reasonably available. A fee-free manual bank transfer appears capable of satisfying this requirement, even if it is slower. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

The provider or agent must also tell you about costs, including **third-party transaction fees and electronic-payment-facility fees**, before you consent to use that payment method. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

The Act separately says that a person must not demand or receive a charge, or an indemnity for a charge, for establishing or using **any electronic payment facility** to pay rent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) On the documents retrieved, this means the card fee is not made lawful merely because it is described as an app or card-processing fee.

It does **not appear to matter whether the fee is retained by the app company or paid to the agent**: the relevant prohibition applies to “a person”, and the fee-free-payment obligation applies to the rental provider or agent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) However, the retrieved documents do not expressly discuss the precise contractual relationship between an app company, agent and renter, so they do not provide a more detailed answer about the app company’s separate liability.

The prescribed payment method that must be permitted is **electronic funds transfer**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) The standard rental agreement also states that at least one payment method must be fee-free, excluding only the renter’s own bank fees. ## What the law says

On **15 October 2019**, the applicable document was **_Residential Tenancies Act 1997_, Authorised Version 088, dated 2 July 2019** (“AV 088”). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

The landlord had to ensure that, on the agreed occupation day, the premises were **vacant and reasonably clean**. You were not required to enter into occupation if they did not meet that requirement, and you did not have to pay rent for the period before you actually entered into occupation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

The landlord also had a continuing duty to maintain the premises in **good repair**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) Damp, mould and rotting timber may amount to repair or safety problems, but the retrieved document does not specifically classify those particular defects.

If you **had not entered into possession**, you could give the landlord a notice terminating the tenancy on the ground that the premises were **not in good repair**, **unfit for human habitation**, **unsafe**, **not vacant**, **not legally available as a residence**, or otherwise **unavailable for occupation**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask to cancel by agreement.**  
   You can ask the landlord to agree in writing to terminate the tenancy; the Act expressly permits termination by agreement. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) If the landlord agrees, obtain written confirmation about termination, keys, bond and any rent already paid.

2. **Give a statutory termination notice if you have not entered into possession.**  
   If you have not actually entered into possession, you can give a notice of termination relying on the relevant ground—for example, that the premises are not in good repair or are unavailable for occupation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) The document does not prescribe a particular notice period for section 226, so it does not provide a precise period to state here.

3. **Ask for repairs.**  
   Give the landlord written notice describing the damp, mould and rotting timber and request repairs. The landlord’s duty is to maintain the premises in good repair. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) For non-urgent repairs, if the landlord does not act within **14 days** after written notice, the tenant may apply to the Director for an investigation; after receiving the Director’s report, the tenant may apply to the Tribunal for a repair order. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

4. **Ask for lower rent.**  
   You may ask the landlord to agree to a lower rent, but the retrieved document does not give an automatic right to a rent reduction merely because defects were found. The statutory excessive-rent process applies where services, facilities or other items have been reduced or withdrawn, or where the tenant has received a rent-increase notice; the state of repair and general condition of the premises are matters the Tribunal considers. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

5. **Do not simply stop paying rent without an order or agreement.**  
   The document provides a formal mechanism for applying to the Tribunal to pay rent into the **Rent Special Account** after notice requiring repairs has been given and the landlord has failed to comply; it does not state that a tenant may unilaterally withhold rent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

**Practical position:** document the defects with photographs and written descriptions, notify the landlord immediately, and ask either for written cancellation and repayment of any money paid, or for a written repair plan. The retrieved document does not say whether merely collecting the keys counts as having “entered into possession”; that fact may affect whether section 226 is available.

Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic), Authorised Version v088**, which was in force on 15 October 2019 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf), here is how the law applies to your situation:

### 🔑 Can I cancel?
The provided text does not explicitly grant a statutory right to "cancel" a lease before possession. However, you have a strong legal right to **refuse to move in** until the issues are fixed. 
* Under section 65(1), a landlord must ensure the premises are vacant and in a reasonably clean condition on the agreed occupation day [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Damp, mould, and rotting timber likely breach this standard.
* Under section 65(2), you are **not required to enter into occupation** if the premises do not comply with that requirement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). 
* If you refuse to move in, section 65(3) states you **do not have to pay rent** for the period from the agreed occupation day until the day you actually enter [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

### 🛠️ Can I ask for repairs?
Yes. The landlord has a clear legal duty to fix these issues.
* Section 68(1) requires the landlord to ensure the rented premises are maintained in good repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Damp, mould, and rotting timber fall squarely under this maintenance obligation.
* You should give the landlord **written notice** specifying that these non-urgent repairs are required [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
* If the landlord does not carry out the repairs within **14 days** of receiving your notice, you can apply to the Director to investigate the breach (section 74) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Following the Director's report, you can then apply to VCAT for a formal order requiring the landlord to carry out the specified repairs (section 75) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

### 💰 Can I ask for lower rent?
The Act does not provide a mechanism to simply "ask" a landlord for a voluntary rent reduction. However, it provides two financial protections relevant to your situation:
1. **Rent suspension until entry:** If you refuse to move in due to the poor condition, you legally owe $0 rent from the agreed start date until you actually take possession [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
2. **Rent Special Account:** If you do move in and give notice for repairs that the landlord then ignores, you can apply to VCAT under section 77 for an order authorising you to pay your rent into a Rent Special Account instead of directly to the landlord [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). This holds the funds until the repair obligations are met or the matter is resolved.

### 📝 Immediate Steps You Should Take
* **Do not sign off on a clean condition report.** Section 35 requires the landlord to give you two copies of a condition report before you enter occupation, and you have 3 business days after entering to return one with endorsements [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Since you haven't moved in yet, explicitly note the damp, mould, and rotting timber on the report before signing it.
* **Document everything.** Take dated photos/videos of the defects and keep copies of all written communication with the landlord/agent regarding these issues.

*Note: This answer is based strictly on the provided excerpts from the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic) v088 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). For complex disputes or if the landlord refuses to address the condition, contacting VCAT or a community legal centre for tailored advice is recommended.*

Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic)**, Authorised Version No. 101 (in force on 8 November 2022) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf), here is what you should check and verify before paying rent into the new account:

### 1. Written Notice of New Contact Details
Because the owner is now managing the property themselves (meaning there is no longer an agent acting for them), they are legally required to provide you with written notice containing:
*   Their full name and address for the service of documents [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
*   An emergency telephone number for urgent repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

The owner must give you this written notice before the end of the day after the change takes effect [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). Do not pay into a new account until you have received this formal notification.

### 2. Agreement to Change Payment Method
Your rent is payable in the manner specified in your residential rental agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). Paying into a completely different bank account constitutes a change to how rent is payable. 
*   You should ensure that **both you and the owner formally agree** to this change in writing [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). 
*   Once agreed, the new bank details should ideally be added as an addendum or written variation to your lease agreement to protect your payment history.

### 3. Bond Lodgement Details
Even though the management has changed, your bond must remain lodged with the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority (RTBA) under the correct residential rental provider's name [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). 
*   If the owner is taking over the rights and duties from the agency or a previous landlord, they are legally required to notify the RTBA of this assignment/transfer within 5 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
*   You have the right to receive a copy of this notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). Check that your bond records accurately reflect the new owner's name.

### 4. Receipts for Future Payments
Once you start paying into the new account, ensure the owner complies with receipt requirements:
*   If you pay in person, they must give you a written receipt immediately [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
*   If you pay electronically or by mail and request a receipt at the time of payment, they must provide it within 5 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). 
*   The receipt must state your name, the rented premises, the date, the period covered, the amount paid, and clearly state that the payment is for rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

**Summary of Action:** Do not transfer the money until you have received written confirmation of the owner's new contact details, a signed agreement to change the payment method, and verification that your bond records with the RTBA are being updated correctly.

**Short answer:** Probably not. Under the version of the Act in force on 15 January 2026, a landlord or agent must keep a no-extra-cost payment method reasonably available, and the law generally bars charging a fee for paying rent electronically. Whether a fee charged by a third-party app is covered is less clear from the text.

**Which law applies:** The Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 111 (in force from 25 November 2025 to 29 June 2026), is the version for your date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). A later Version 115 is dated from 13 October 2026, so it does not apply to you [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What the law says**

- **Fee-free method must be available.** The provider or agent must ensure a rent payment method that "incurs no additional costs (other than bank fees or account fees payable on the renter's bank account) is reasonably available to the renter" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Your manual bank transfer appears to meet this. The text says nothing about speed, so being slower does not by itself make it unavailable.
- **No charge for electronic payment facilities.** A person "must not demand or receive from a renter a charge or indemnity for a charge in relation to... the use of... any other electronic payment facility for payment of rent" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The penalty is 60 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). This wording does not limit the charge to the landlord or agent.
- **Fees by businesses.** A business other than a provider, an agent, or an authorised deposit-taking institution must not "demand or receive a fee for any prescribed matter" in relation to paying rent. The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person or 400 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The app company is not one of the exempt categories [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). However, the retrieved text does not list which matters are "prescribed," so I cannot confirm that a card fee is one of them.
- **Disclosure.** Before you agree to a payment method, the provider or agent must tell you about costs you may incur, including "third party transaction fees" and "any other electronic payment facility fees" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**Does it matter who receives the fee?**

The documents suggest it may matter, but they do not settle it:

- The s 51A exemption covers the provider and agent, so an agent's fee falls outside that section [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The s 51(3)(b) ban on electronic payment charges, however, applies to "a person" generally [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- Section 42(7) refers to third-party transaction fees as costs the renter "may incur," which suggests the Act expects some third-party costs to exist and must be disclosed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Whether an app's fee is a banned charge or only a disclosable one is not answered by the retrieved text.

**What you can do**

1. Ask the agent in writing for the exact fee and who receives it, as s 42(7) requires disclosure before you consent to a method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
2. Ask them to confirm that the bank transfer option is available and fee-free, as s 42(4) requires [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The Regulations' standard form also says the provider "must permit a fee-free (other than the renter's own bank fees) payment method" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
3. If they refuse, you can raise it with Consumer Affairs Victoria or apply to VCAT. The retrieved documents do not describe those steps in detail, so check them directly.
4. Ask for a written receipt. If you request one when paying, it must be given within 5 business days, and the penalty for not providing it is 25 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**Limits of this answer:** The documents do not say whether a particular app's card fee is a "prescribed matter" or a banned "electronic payment facility" charge. A tenancy adviser or VCAT would need to decide that for your specific fee.

**Short answer:** The retrieved documents do not contain enough to answer whether you can cancel, or whether you can get a rent reduction, for conditions found before you move in. They do show that damp, mould and structural faults can count as urgent repairs, and that the Act's protections cannot be contracted out of.

**Version applied:** On 15 October 2019, the version in force is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Authorised Version No. 088), which applied from 2 July 2019 to 3 December 2019 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The later versions (No. 101 from 2022 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf) and No. 111 from 2025 [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)) and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) were not in force on that date, so I have not relied on them.

**What the law says**

- The Act's objectives include "safe and habitable premises" for renters [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- "Urgent repairs" includes "any fault or damage that makes rented premises... unsafe or insecure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The 2019 text of that definition, as shown in the retrieved excerpt, does not expressly list mould or damp. Text that does list "the presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure" appears in the amendment provisions in the same document [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf), and the later version lists it expressly [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). I could not confirm from the excerpt when that amendment took effect, so you should check this before relying on it.
- A term in a lease that purports to exclude or restrict the Act's provisions, or the exercise of a right under the Act, is invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- For urgent repairs, the "required time" for a duty under section 60 or 67 is 7 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The excerpt does not say what sections 60 or 67 require.

**Your options, as far as the documents show**

- **Repairs:** The documents support treating serious damp or structural faults as a matter for the landlord to repair, and the 7-day "required time" applies to the section 60 and 67 duties [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The excerpt does not set out the step-by-step repair request process, and I cannot confirm that the timeframe applies to your specific defects.
- **Lower rent:** The Act says a lease must not include a term reducing rent if the renter does not breach the agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). That concerns lease terms, not a tribunal's power to reduce rent for defects. The documents do not say whether you can seek a rent reduction for these conditions, so I cannot answer this part.
- **Cancelling:** The documents do not include a provision allowing you to end a lease because of conditions found before move-in. I cannot answer this part from them.

**What I could not find:** the 2019 minimum standards for mould and dampness (the 2021 Regulations contain one, but they were not in force on 15 October 2019 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)); the procedure for issuing a repair request; and any early-termination or rent-reduction remedy. The Tribunal, which is the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf), is the body that resolves disputes under the Act, but the documents do not describe the process for bringing a claim. A lawyer or the Tribunal should confirm the remedies available to you before you act.

## Short answer

The version in force on 15 October 2019 was the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version 088 (file "rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf", in force 2 July 2019 to 3 December 2019) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The extract I retrieved from it is only endnote text reproducing amending provisions. It does not show the operative sections on premises condition, cancelling or rent. The operative wording below comes from later versions, so I can't confirm it matched the law on 15 October 2019.

## What the law says

Version 090 (file "rta-1997-v090-2020-03-02.pdf", dated 2 March 2020) is a later version, and the wording below comes from it:

- **Condition at move-in:** the landlord must ensure that on the agreed day the tenant enters occupation, the premises are "vacant and in a reasonably clean condition" (s 65(1)) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf). The section only mentions vacancy and cleanliness. It doesn't mention damp, mould or rotting timber.
- **Ongoing repairs duty:** a landlord "must ensure that the rented premises are maintained in good repair" (s 68(1)) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

**1. Cancel or refuse to move in**
- Under s 65(2), a tenant "is not required to enter into occupation" of premises that fail the s 65(1) standard [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf).
- That only helps if the problem counts as a failure of vacancy or reasonable cleanliness. The text doesn't say whether damp or mould does.
- I found nothing in the retrieved documents on ending a lease for pre-move-in defects, such as a notice to vacate or a VCAT termination order. The documents don't answer whether you can cancel.

**2. Ask for repairs**
- **Non-urgent repairs:**
  - Give the landlord written notice that repairs are needed.
  - If they aren't done within 14 days, you can apply to the Director to investigate (s 74) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa097%20authorised.pdf).
  - After the Director's report, you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring specified repairs (s 75) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa097%20authorised.pdf).
  - The later amending text in versions 088 and 089 also lets a renter apply to VCAT directly after the 14 days, and says VCAT must hear it within 7 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf). The retrieved extract doesn't show when that took effect, so I can't confirm it applied on 15 October 2019.
- **Urgent repairs:**
  - You may arrange urgent repairs yourself if you've taken reasonable steps to get the landlord to do them immediately and couldn't (s 72(1)) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf).
  - You must give 14 days' written notice of the repairs and cost, and the landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost or $1000, whichever is less (s 72(2)) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf).
  - If you can't afford the repairs, they cost more than $1000, or the landlord refuses to pay, you can apply to VCAT. It must hear the application within 2 business days (s 73) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa097%20authorised.pdf).
  - The retrieved text doesn't say whether damp, mould or rotting timber count as "urgent". The urgent repairs definition I found is in a 2026 version (v115) and doesn't apply to 15 October 2019 [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Rent into the Rent Special Account:** once you've given notice requiring repairs, you can apply to VCAT to pay your rent into the Rent Special Account (s 77) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa097%20authorised.pdf).

**3. Ask for lower rent**
- The retrieved documents don't give a direct right to a reduction for defects.
- **Rent for the delay in moving in:** if the premises fail s 65(1), you don't have to pay rent from the agreed occupation day until the day you actually move in (s 65(3)) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf).
- **Excessive rent:** a tenant can ask the Director to investigate rent considered excessive because the landlord has reduced or withdrawn services or facilities, or because of a rent increase (s 45) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa097%20authorised.pdf).
  - VCAT can then declare rent excessive, with "the state of repair and general condition of the rented premises" as one factor (s 47(3)(b)) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa097%20authorised.pdf).
  - These are from version 097 (28 March 2021), which is later than your date. They concern excessive rent, not a defects-based reduction.

## Gaps
The retrieved documents don't confirm the exact wording of these sections on 15 October 2019, and they don't cover cancelling a lease. For those points, please check Version 088 directly or ask Consumer Affairs Victoria or VCAT.

# Paying rent to a new account after the agent hands over to the owner (as at 8 November 2022)

**Documents used:**
- *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v101-2022-09-07.pdf", in force 7 Sept 2022 to 23 May 2023, so it covers 8 Nov 2022. Its metadata gives the version as 101. The excerpts I retrieved don't print an "Authorised Version No." line, so I'm relying on that metadata.
- *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, file "rt-regs-2021-v002-2022-06-01.pdf", in force 1 June 2022 to 30 Nov 2024.

## What the law says

- **A change from agent to owner must be notified in writing.** If an agent acts for the provider, the provider must give the renter written notice of the agent's name, address for service and phone details. If there is no agent, the provider must give written notice of their own full name, address for service of documents and an emergency phone number. The provider must give written notice of any change in this information within 7 days after the change. The penalty is 60 penalty units (s 66(2)–(4)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **The standard lease form says the same.** Form 1 (the standard residential rental agreement) lists the provider's and agent's details. It notes that the provider must tell the renter within 7 days if any of them change [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). It also says the parties must immediately notify each other in writing if their contact details change [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **The lease form also covers payment.** Form 1 has a section for the provider's preferred payment methods and payment details. It says the provider must permit a fee-free payment method (other than the renter's own bank fees). It also says the provider must allow Centrepay or another form of electronic funds transfer. The renter is entitled to a receipt confirming payment of rent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

## What you can check or ask

1. **Get the change in writing.** Ask for written notice from the owner, not only from the agent. It should give the owner's full name, address for service and an emergency number [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
2. **Compare it with your lease.** Check the payment details and the provider and agent details in your signed agreement, if it's on Form 1 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Ask for the new account details in writing and keep a copy.
3. **Ask about costs and methods.** Confirm that a fee-free payment option is available and that Centrepay or electronic transfer is allowed [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Ask for a receipt.** The lease form says you're entitled to one [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
5. **Check your bond.** You've already paid it, so check that the bond was lodged. The provider (which includes an agent) must lodge it with the Authority within 10 business days of receiving it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). If you haven't received an Authority receipt within 15 business days, you may notify the Authority [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't cover

- **Receipts and payment method rules (ss 42–43).** The text of these sections in the 2022 version (v101) wasn't in what I retrieved. I only found them in later versions (2025 and 2026), which don't apply to your date. I haven't relied on those versions.

## What the law says — 15 January 2026

The applicable document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 111, in force from 25 November 2025 to 29 June 2026**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

- The rental provider or agent must ensure that a rent-payment method with **no additional cost**—apart from bank or account fees payable on your own bank account—is **reasonably available**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- Therefore, if the manual bank transfer is genuinely available and has no fee, the app may generally charge a fee for choosing card payment; the law does not require every payment method to be fee-free. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- Before you consent to use a payment method, the rental provider or agent must tell you about costs you may incur, including **third-party transaction fees** and **electronic payment facility fees**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- Separately, no person may demand or receive a charge for the **establishment or use of an electronic payment facility for rent**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) The retrieved document does not expressly resolve whether this prohibits the particular card surcharge you describe, as opposed to a fee for establishing or using the facility.
- On 15 January 2026, the later regulation prohibiting prescribed rent-payment fees was **not yet in force**: the retrieved regulations say regulation 21C applies only **on and after 31 March 2026**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Its later wording also excludes “payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act,” but that later rule cannot be applied to 15 January 2026. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

### Does it matter who receives the fee?

The documents do **not** provide a clear answer that makes the result depend on whether the fee goes to the app company or the agent. Section 42 applies to the rental provider or agent’s obligation to provide a fee-free method and disclose costs, while section 51(3) refers broadly to **“a person”**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

Ask the agent, in writing:

1. **What is the exact card fee and who receives it?**
2. **Is the bank-transfer option genuinely available without any fee?**
3. **Was the fee disclosed before you consented to use the card method?**
4. **Is the fee for using the electronic payment facility, or only a separately identified third-party transaction surcharge?**

answer:
**Governing version:** The Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 088 (incorporating amendments as at 2 July 2019), is the version in force on 15 October 2019. Its metadata gives an in-force period of 2 July 2019 to 3 December 2019 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Condition on move-in day:** The landlord must ensure that on the day you are to move in, the premises are vacant and reasonably clean. If they are not, you are not required to move in, and you do not have to pay rent from the agreed move-in day until the day you actually move in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (s 65).
- **Repair duty:** The landlord must ensure the premises are "maintained in good repair" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (s 68(1)).
- **Damp and mould:** The amendment text in the endnotes adds "the presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure" to the definition of urgent repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The retrieved documents do not confirm when that amendment took effect, so check whether it applied on 15 October 2019.

## Can you cancel?

The retrieved material does not answer this. The table of provisions lists "Termination by tenant before possession" (s 226) and "Premises destroyed or unfit for habitation" (s 238) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf), but I could not retrieve their text. I can't confirm a right to cancel from these documents. What I can say is that s 65 means you are not required to move in and owe no rent for the period before you actually move in, if the premises don't meet the move-in standard [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

## Can you ask for repairs?

Yes. The steps in the document are:

1. **Give written notice.** You must give the landlord written notice that repairs (other than urgent repairs) are needed. If the landlord does not carry them out within 14 days, you can apply to the Director to investigate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (s 74).
2. **Urgent repairs.** If you have taken reasonable steps to get the landlord to repair them immediately and cannot get them done, you may arrange the repairs yourself. You must give the landlord 14 days' written notice of the repairs and their cost. The landlord must then reimburse the reasonable cost or $1,000, whichever is less [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (s 72). The endnote amendment changes the reimbursement period to 7 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf), but I cannot confirm that it applied on 15 October 2019.
3. **Tribunal orders.** You can apply to the Tribunal for an urgent-repair order if you cannot meet the cost, the repairs cost more than $1,000, or the landlord refuses to pay. The Tribunal must hear the application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (s 73). For non-urgent repairs, you can apply within 60 days of receiving the Director's report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (s 75). The Tribunal can order the landlord to carry out specified repairs within a specified time [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (s 76).
4. **Rent into the Rent Special Account.** After you have given repair notice and the landlord has failed to comply, you can apply to the Tribunal to pay rent into the Rent Special Account [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (s 77).

## Can you ask for lower rent?

Yes, but the route is a complaint or application about **excessive rent**. You may complain to the Director about excessive rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (s 45) or apply to the Tribunal [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (s 46). In deciding what rent is reasonable, the Tribunal must have regard to the state of repair and general condition of the premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (s 47(1)(b)). If the Tribunal makes an order, the landlord cannot require rent above the ordered amount for 12 months [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (s 47(4)), and the Tribunal may order a refund of the difference from the date you applied [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (s 48).

## Summary and limits

- You are not required to move in until the premises are reasonably clean, and you pay no rent until you do [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- You can demand repairs in writing, then go to the Director or the Tribunal [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- You can ask for a lower rent through the excessive-rent provisions [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- The documents I retrieved do not show whether you can cancel the agreement, because the relevant termination provisions were not in the retrieved text.

This is general information based only on the retrieved Act, not legal advice. For a decision about cancelling or a dispute, get advice from the Director or the Tribunal.

answer:
**What the law says (as at 3 December 2025)**

The Residential Tenancies Act 1997 is in Authorised Version No. 111, incorporating amendments as at 25 November 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 are in version 005 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Both were in force on 3 December 2025.

- **Renter's duty:** A renter must permit a person exercising a right of entry under the Act to enter the premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Smoke alarm duty:** The landlord must ensure each smoke alarm is tested at least once every 12 months, in line with the manufacturer's instructions [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). A smoke alarm check can therefore be a lawful reason for entry.
- **Timing and notice:** For this purpose, entry is allowed at any time between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. on any day except a public holiday, if at least 24 hours' notice has been given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Entry can also happen at any time the renter agrees, if the renter consented within 7 days before the entry [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Notice requirements:** The notice must be in writing, state why the landlord or agent wants to enter, and be given by post or delivered personally between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Manner of entry:** The person entering must act reasonably and must not stay longer than necessary [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**Do you have to be there yourself?**

The documents do not say whether the renter must be personally present. They say the renter must *permit* lawful entry [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), and they don't address whether the renter has to be home. If you can't be there, the documents don't give a rule either way, so I can't confirm whether your presence is required.

**Can they charge $90 to rebook?**

The documents contain no provision allowing a rebooking fee. They also don't mention the agent's 10 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. window. The Act's entry window is 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). A landlord or agent must not demand or accept payment from a renter who has failed to comply with the agreement or the Act, other than rent or an amount or penalty provided for in the Act [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). I haven't retrieved the text of section 51 ("Certain charges prohibited"), so I can't confirm whether it covers this fee. I also can't tell from the documents whether the $90 appears in your tenancy agreement.

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Ask for the notice in writing.** It must state why entry is needed, be in writing, and be given by post or personally delivered between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Check that it gives at least 24 hours' notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
2. **Propose a time.** Entry at an agreed time is allowed if you consented within 7 days before the entry [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
3. **Ask for the legal basis of the $90 fee in writing.** The documents don't show any authority for it.
4. **Apply to VCAT to limit entry.** You may apply to the Tribunal for an order specifying or limiting the days, times and purposes of entry [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
5. **Seek protection if entry breaks the rules.** You may apply to the Tribunal for an order restraining entry for a specified period [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), or for compensation if damage is caused to your goods during entry [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
6. **Get more information.** The regulations refer to consumer.vic.gov.au/renting for more information [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

**Short answer:** Under the law in force on 8 November 2022, a change to how rent is paid needs your agreement, and the new method must meet the rules below. The documents I found don't say how to verify a bank account, so you'll need to confirm the details independently.

## What the law says

- **Change must be agreed.** The Act says that the rental provider and renter, "by agreement, may change the manner in which rent is payable" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The agent saying the owner will manage the property and has new bank details doesn't, on its face, change your agreement.
- **Payment place and method.** Rent is payable at the place specified in the agreement, or at the rented premises if none is specified [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). Where the agreement sets the payment manner, rent is payable in that manner [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **No extra costs.** The rental provider or their agent "must ensure that a rent payment method that incurs no additional costs (other than bank fees or account fees payable on the renter's bank account) is reasonably available to the renter" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Cost information first.** Before you consent to a payment method, the provider or agent must tell you about any costs you may incur, including third-party transaction fees and direct debit dishonour fees [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Centrepay.** The provider or agent must permit payment by Centrepay [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **No post-dated cheques.** Rent cannot be required by post-dated cheque or other post-dated negotiable instrument [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Who counts as the provider.** The definition of "residential rental provider" includes an agent of the provider [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The agent's notice is therefore given on the owner's behalf, but the agreement and payment rules still apply.

## What the renter can check or ask

1. **Your consent.** Don't treat the agent's message as a change to your agreement. Ask for the change in writing and agree to it only if you accept it.
2. **Fees.** Ask whether the new account incurs any fee beyond your own bank fees, and ask for the cost information the Act requires before you agree [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
3. **Payment options.** Ask whether Centrepay and a fee-free method are available. The prescribed agreement form says the provider "must permit at least one fee-free (other than the renter's own bank fees) payment method and must allow the renter to use Centrepay or another form of electronic funds transfer" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Receipts.** You are entitled to a receipt confirming rent payment [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). If you pay without being in person, you can request a receipt at the time of payment, and it must be given within 5 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The receipt must be signed and must state your name and the premises, the date of receipt, the period paid, the amount, and that the payment is for rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
5. **Bond.** Check the bond is lodged. The provider must lodge the bond with the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority within 10 business days after receiving it . The Authority must send a receipt within 7 days . If you don't receive a receipt within 15 business days of paying the bond, you may email rtba@justice.vic.gov.au or call 1300 137 164 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
6. **Change of owner or agent.** The prescribed form notes that the provider must tell the renter within 7 days if agent details change [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). If the owner takes over the rights and duties under the agreement and a bond was paid, the owner and the new person must notify the Authority within 5 days, and the provider must give you a copy of the notice .

## What the documents don't cover

- How to verify that the bank account belongs to the owner, or how to spot payment fraud. Confirm the account details directly with the owner or the agent through contact details you already have, not through the new message.
- Whether the owner must be named on the account.
