answer:
## What the law says (as at 15 January 2026)

**Documents applied:**
- *rta-1997-v111-2025-11-25.pdf* (Residential Tenancies Act 1997, version 111, dated 25 Nov 2025, in force to 29 June 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- *rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf* (Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, version 005, dated 25 Nov 2025, in force to 9 Feb 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

The documents give version numbers, not the words "Authorised Version No." The version numbers above come from the file names and metadata.

**1. A free payment method must be reasonably available.** The rental provider or their agent must make sure a rent payment method with no additional costs is reasonably available to you. Your own bank or account fees don't count as additional costs. The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person and 400 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The standard rental agreement form repeats this: a fee-free method (other than your own bank fees) must be permitted [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The documents don't define "reasonably available", so I can't say whether "slower" makes a bank transfer unreasonable.

**2. You must be told about costs first.** The provider or agent must give you information about any costs, including third-party transaction fees and other electronic payment facility fees. They must do this before you consent to using that payment method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**3. There is a ban on charges for electronic payment facilities.** Under s 51(3)(b), "a person" must not demand or receive from a renter a charge for "the establishment or use of direct debit facilities or any other electronic payment facility for payment of rent". The penalty is 60 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether a card option in a rent app counts as an "electronic payment facility". If it does, this section could stop the card fee even though a free transfer exists. I can't confirm that from the documents.

## Does it matter who gets the fee?

- **Sections 42(4) and 42(7)** only bind the rental provider and their agent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Section 51(3)** applies to "a person", so it isn't limited to the agent. It could cover an app company as well [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Section 51A** bans a business (other than a rental provider, their agent, or a bank) from charging a fee for a "prescribed matter" relating to rent payment. That is aimed at third parties like an app company. The penalty is 80 or 400 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
  - The regulation that prescribes "rent payment (other than payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act)" only takes effect **on and after 31 March 2026** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
  - So on 15 January 2026, the documents don't show s 51A catching an app's card fee yet.
  - The documents don't say which "other Act" permits surcharges.

## What you can do

- **Ask in writing** which payment methods are fee-free, and for the full cost details of the card option, before you agree to it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Stick with the free bank transfer.** Nothing in the documents lets an agent force you onto a fee-charging method. The rules require a fee-free option to be available [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Query the card fee itself** under s 51(3)(b), particularly if the agent receives the fee [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Check the agreement.** A term requiring you to pay rent in advance by a method with extra costs is a prescribed prohibited term [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't cover how to complain or enforce these rules, so I can't advise on that. They also don't include any version of the Regulations after 9 February 2026.

**Document used:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 088, "rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf", incorporating amendments as at 2 July 2019. Its metadata shows it in force from 2 July 2019 to 3 December 2019, so it covers 15 October 2019 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **The landlord must keep the premises in good repair.** The landlord "must ensure that the rented premises are maintained in good repair" (s 68) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Handover condition.** On the agreed move-in day the premises must be vacant and in a "reasonably clean condition". A tenant isn't required to move in if they aren't, and doesn't pay rent from the agreed day until they actually move in (s 65) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). This section is about vacancy and cleanliness. The retrieved text doesn't mention damp, mould or rot in it.
- **Ending the agreement before you take possession.** The agreement terminates if you have not entered into possession and you give the landlord a notice of termination on the ground that the premises are "not in good repair", "unfit for human habitation" or "for any other reason unavailable for occupation" (s 226) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Unfit for habitation.** A tenant can also give a notice of intention to vacate if the premises are unfit for human habitation or unsafe. The notice can take effect on the day it is given or later (s 238) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

## Your three options

**1. Cancel**
- Section 226 is the most relevant provision, because you haven't moved in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- You would give written notice of termination to the landlord. The ground would be that the premises are not in good repair or are unfit for habitation. Written notice is my suggestion; s 226 as retrieved doesn't say how the notice must be given.
- The documents don't say whether collecting the keys counts as "entering into possession". They don't define the term, so I can't say whether s 226 or s 238 is the safer route.
- I also can't tell you whether damp, mould and rotting timber amount to "unfit for human habitation". The retrieved text doesn't define that phrase.

**2. Ask for repairs**
- **Urgent repairs (s 72–73):**
  - You may arrange urgent repairs yourself if you have taken reasonable steps to get the landlord or agent to do them immediately and couldn't.
  - You must then give the landlord 14 days' written notice of the repairs and the cost. The landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost, or $1000, whichever is less.
  - If you can't meet the cost, the repairs cost more than $1000, or the landlord refuses to pay, you can apply to the Tribunal. It must hear the application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
  - The definition of "urgent repairs" wasn't in the retrieved text, so I can't confirm that mould, damp or rot qualifies.
- **Non-urgent repairs (s 74–76):**
  1. Give the landlord written notice that repairs are needed.
  2. If they aren't done within 14 days, apply in writing to the Director, who must investigate and give you a written report.
  3. Apply to the Tribunal within 60 days of receiving the report. You can also apply without a report if you haven't received one within 90 days of applying for it.
  4. The Tribunal can order specified repairs, with a deadline, if the landlord is in breach of the duty to maintain the premises in good repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Rent into the Rent Special Account (s 77):** after you have given notice requiring repairs, you can apply to the Tribunal to pay rent into this account. The Tribunal may order it if the landlord has failed to do the repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Exception (s 80):** you can't use ss 72–75 where the breach results from a declaration under s 64 of the *Housing Act 1983* that the house is unfit for habitation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**3. Ask for lower rent**
- The retrieved text has no provision letting a tenant reduce rent on their own because of disrepair.
- The nearest provisions are the excessive-rent provisions. Under s 46, a tenant can apply to the Tribunal for an order declaring rent or proposed rent excessive, after a Director's report under s 45. A tenant who has received a rent increase notice can also apply, with the Tribunal's leave, under s 46(3). The Tribunal must declare the rent excessive if it is more than should reasonably be paid, having regard to factors that include "the state of repair and general condition of the rented premises" (s 47(3)(b)). It can direct a maximum rent for 12 months and order a refund (ss 47–48) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- The parts of s 45 that set out when a tenant can complain about the starting rent weren't retrieved. I can't confirm this route fits your situation.
- Section 65(3) only waives rent between the agreed move-in day and actual occupation. It applies where the premises weren't vacant and reasonably clean [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

## A caveat about the text

The same document also contains amending-Act text in its endnotes, using terms such as "renter" and "residential rental provider". Those passages include a new s 91L and a wider definition of urgent repairs that mentions mould and damp. The retrieved text doesn't show that these were in force on 15 October 2019, so I haven't relied on them. I've used the operative sections quoted above [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

I'd recommend getting advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy advocate before you send any notice. The documents don't answer whether collecting the keys means you have taken possession.

**Documents used:** *rta-1997-v111-2025-11-25.pdf* is the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 111, incorporating amendments as at 25 November 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Its metadata shows it in force from 25 Nov 2025 to 29 Jun 2026, so it was the version in force on 3 December 2025. I also checked *rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf*, the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021. Its metadata labels it version 005 and shows it in force from 25 Nov 2025 to 9 Feb 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

**Smoke alarm duty.** The rental provider must make sure any smoke alarm is correctly installed, working, fitted with batteries, and tested at least once every 12 months [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). This is s 68AA.

**Right of entry.**
- The provider or agent may enter at a time you've agreed to, if you consented within the 7 days before entry [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- Otherwise they may enter between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. on any day except a public holiday, with notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- Entry to carry out a duty under the Act needs at least 24 hours' notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). A smoke alarm test seems to fall here, since it is a duty under s 68AA. That is my reading, not wording in the documents.
- A routine inspection needs at least 7 days' notice, and can't be done if one was made in the last 6 months [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- The notice must be in writing, say why they want to enter, and be given by post or delivered personally between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- They must enter in a reasonable manner and not stay longer than necessary [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**Do you have to be home?** The retrieved provisions don't say so. You have a duty to *permit* entry that complies with the Division [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). That means you must not block a lawful entry. Nothing in the retrieved text requires you to be present to let the inspector in. The provisions also don't say how entry is physically carried out, such as with a key, so they don't answer that. A 10 am–12:30 pm window is within the 8 a.m.–6 p.m. hours, but the documents don't give a "weekday-only" rule [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**Can they charge $90?** The documents I retrieved don't answer this.
- Nothing in the retrieved provisions authorises a rebooking fee for a missed entry.
- The Act's contents list includes s 51, "Certain charges prohibited", and s 51A on certain application and rent payment fees [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The text of those sections wasn't retrieved, so I can't say whether they cover this fee.

## What you can do or ask

- **Ask for the notice in writing.** It should state the purpose and give at least 24 hours' notice, or 7 days if it's really a general inspection [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Offer an agreed time.** If you agree a time within 7 days of entry, they can enter then [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Ask the agent for the legal basis of the $90 fee.** The retrieved documents don't show one.
- **If they enter without following the rules,** you can apply to the Tribunal for an order restraining entry for a set period [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Entering otherwise than in accordance with the Division, without reasonable excuse, is an offence with a penalty of 60 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **If you need to limit when entry happens,** you can apply to the Tribunal for an order specifying or limiting entry times [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Check s 51 yourself.** I'd confirm the fee question against the full text of s 51 of the Act. The standard agreement also lists the rental provider's safety duties, including smoke alarms [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

I haven't seen your agreement or the agent's notice, so I can't say whether this particular notice complies.

# Rent paid to new bank details after a switch from agent to owner (Victoria, as at 8 November 2022)

**Sources used:** *rta-1997-v101-2022-09-07.pdf* (Residential Tenancies Act 1997, version 101, in force 7 Sep 2022 to 23 May 2023, so it covers 8 Nov 2022) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). I also used *rt-regs-2021-v002-2022-06-01.pdf* (Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, version 002, in force from 1 Jun 2022) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The excerpts I retrieved don't print an "Authorised Version No." line. The version numbers above come from the documents' metadata.

## What the law says

- **Rent follows the agreement.** Rent is payable at the place and in the manner specified in the agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The rental provider and renter can change the manner of payment *by agreement* [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether a new bank account counts as a change of "manner", so check what your lease says.
- **Changes of agent or contact details need written notice.** If an agent is acting, the provider must give the renter the agent's name, address for service and phone/fax numbers. If there is no agent, the provider must give their own full name, address for service and an emergency phone number [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). Any change in that information must be notified in writing within 7 days of the change. The penalty is 60 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The standard lease form carries the same 7-day note [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Payment options.** The provider or their agent must make a payment method with no extra cost (other than your own bank fees) reasonably available. They must also allow Centrepay and any prescribed method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). They must tell you about any costs of a payment method before you consent to it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Receipts.** Whoever receives rent must give a written receipt immediately if you pay in person. If you don't pay in person, they must give one within 5 business days of a request made when you pay [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The receipt must be signed and state your name and the premises, the date, the period paid, the amount, and that it is for rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). If no receipt is required, the recipient must keep a record for 12 months, and give you a copy within 5 business days of a request [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Bond.** The provider must lodge your bond with the Authority within 10 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The Authority must send you a receipt within 7 days of getting it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). If you haven't had a receipt within 15 business days of paying, you may notify the Authority [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

## What you can check or ask for

1. **Get the change in writing.** Ask for written notice from the owner of the change from agent to owner-managed. It should give the owner's full name, address for service and an emergency phone number [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). A bank-details message alone doesn't meet this.
2. **Check your lease.** Look at the payment details and preferred methods in your agreement [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Ask that any change to how or where you pay be agreed with you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
3. **Confirm the owner's identity.** Compare the owner's name with the provider named in your lease and the bond lodgment form, and with your Authority bond receipt [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). If ownership has actually been transferred, the provider must notify the Authority within 5 days and give you a copy of that notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Ask about costs.** Confirm the new account has no extra fees for you, and ask for fee information before you agree [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
5. **Ask for a receipt every time.** Request a signed receipt with the details listed above when you pay [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
6. **Check your bond.** Confirm you received the Authority's bond receipt [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't cover

- They don't say whether the agent's authority ends on a set date, or whether you can keep paying the agent until you receive proper written notice.
- They contain nothing on verifying bank details or avoiding payment scams. Phoning the agent on a number you already hold, and the owner separately, to confirm the account before paying is my own practical suggestion, not something in these documents.

For a dispute, the documents point to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria and VCAT [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf), but they don't say how either would handle a payment-details problem. I'd suggest getting advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria (1300 558 181, the number given in the lease form [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)).

## What the law says

On **15 January 2026**, the relevant versions were:

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 111, dated 25 November 2025** (“the Act”), in force from 25 November 2025 to 29 June 2026. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 005, dated 25 November 2025**, in force on 15 January 2026. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

The rental provider or agent must make reasonably available **at least one rent-payment method with no additional cost**, apart from bank or account fees payable on the renter’s own bank account. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) A manual bank transfer with no fee appears to satisfy that requirement, even if it is slower. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

They must also tell you, **before you consent to use a payment method**, about costs you may incur, including third-party transaction fees and electronic-payment-facility fees. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

However, section 51(3) prohibits **“a person”** from demanding or receiving a charge for the establishment or use of direct-debit facilities or **any other electronic payment facility for payment of rent**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) The retrieved documents do not definitively say whether this particular card fee is legally characterised as such a prohibited charge or as a permissible third-party transaction fee. Therefore, they do not provide a conclusive yes-or-no answer about the card fee itself.

The newer prohibition on prescribed rent-payment fees does not resolve the position on 15 January: regulation 21C, including “rent payment”, only has effect **on and after 31 March 2026**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

It does **not appear to turn on who ultimately receives the fee**. Section 51(3) applies to “a person”, while the fee-free-method duty applies to the residential rental provider or that person’s agent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) The documents do not contain an exception allowing the fee merely because it is paid to the app company rather than the agent.

## What you can do or ask

Ask the agent or provider, in writing:

1. **What is the legal basis and exact purpose of the card fee?**
2. Is it a fee for using an electronic payment facility, or a third-party transaction fee?
3. **Who receives it**—the app company, agent, or someone else?
4. Confirm that the no-fee bank-transfer option will remain reasonably available.
5. Ask why section 51(3) does not prohibit the fee if it is a charge for using an electronic payment facility for rent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

If the fee is charged by the app company directly, the retrieved documents do not state whether that company is the rental provider’s agent or otherwise determine the fee’s legality. On these documents alone, you should not assume that changing the recipient makes the fee lawful.

answer:
## What the law says

On **15 October 2019**, the applicable document was **_Residential Tenancies Act 1997_ — Authorised Version No. 088, incorporating amendments as at 2 July 2019**. That version was in force from 2 July to 3 December 2019. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

A landlord had to ensure that, on the agreed occupation day, the premises were **vacant and reasonably clean**; a tenant was not required to enter premises that did not meet those requirements, and did not have to pay rent for the period before actually entering occupation if they did not. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) The landlord also had to maintain the premises in **good repair**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

### Can you cancel?

Yes—**if you have not entered into possession**. You may give the landlord a notice terminating the tenancy if the premises:

- are **not in good repair**;
- are **unfit for human habitation**;
- are unsafe;
- are not vacant; or
- are otherwise unavailable for occupation. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

The Act does not state in the retrieved text whether merely collecting the keys amounts to entering into possession. Therefore, the documents do not resolve that factual issue. If the premises are unfit for human habitation or have been rendered unsafe, a tenant may also give a notice of intention to vacate effective immediately or on a later date under section 238. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

Yes. The landlord must maintain the premises in good repair. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

You should give the landlord **written notice** describing the damp, mould and rotting timber and request repairs. For non-urgent repairs, if the landlord has not repaired them within **14 days**, you may apply to the Director for an investigation and report. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) After receiving the report, you may apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring specified repairs; the application generally must be made within **60 days** of receiving the report. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) In that case, after taking reasonable steps to have the landlord or agent act immediately, you may arrange the repairs if you cannot get them to do so; the landlord’s reimbursement obligation is limited to the reasonable cost or **$1,000**, whichever is less. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) You may instead apply to the Tribunal for urgent-repair orders where you cannot meet the cost, the cost exceeds **$1,000**, or the landlord refuses to pay. They do provide a process for challenging **excessive rent**. You may apply to the Director if you consider the rent excessive because the landlord has reduced or withdrawn services, facilities or other items, or after receiving a rent-increase notice. **Practical options under this version:** promptly document the defects with photographs and written descriptions; notify the landlord in writing; and, if you have not entered possession, consider giving a section 226 termination notice rather than moving in. Do not describe the keys issue as settled by the retrieved documents: they do not determine whether collecting keys alone means you entered possession.

**Can the app charge you a card fee?**
Yes, but with a strict condition. The law permits landlords and agents to use payment apps that charge fees (often referred to as "third party transaction fees" or "electronic payment facility fees") [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). As long as a fee-free alternative is provided and you are informed of the costs beforehand, the destination of the fee is not regulated by this section of the Act.

**1. Can you cancel or refuse to move in?**
Yes. Under section 65(1), your landlord is legally required to ensure the premises are vacant and reasonably clean on the day you are supposed to move in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Section 65(2) explicitly states that you are not required to enter into occupation if the premises do not meet this standard [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). If you choose not to move in, section 65(3) confirms you do not have to pay rent for the period between the agreed start date and the day you actually enter (if you eventually do) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**2. Can you ask for repairs?**
Yes. Under section 68(1), a landlord must ensure the rented premises are maintained in good repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). If the damp, mould, and rotting timber mean the premises are not in good repair, you can take these steps under Division 6 of the Act:
* Give the landlord written notice that repairs are required (section 74(1)(a)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
* If the landlord does not carry out the repairs within 14 days, you can apply to the Director to investigate whether the landlord is in breach of their duty (section 74(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
* After receiving the Director's report, if satisfactory arrangements still haven't been made, you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring the landlord to carry out the specified repairs (section 75(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**3. Can you ask for lower rent?**
The Act does not give tenants a direct right to unilaterally demand a lower rent. However, it provides a mechanism for rent relief if the landlord neglects necessary repairs:
* If you have given notice requiring repairs and the landlord fails to comply with their duty, you can apply to VCAT for an order authorising you to pay your rent into a "Rent Special Account" instead of directly to the landlord (section 77(1) and (2)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
* The Tribunal will decide how much rent is held in this account and may later order that some or all of it be paid to the landlord if they fulfill their repair duties (section 77(3)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

### What the law says

- **Change of agent or contact details:** The standard lease forms say the rental provider "must notify the renter within 7 days if any of this information changes," and that information includes the rental provider's details and the agent's details [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). If the owner takes over management, this notice requirement applies.
- **Payment methods:** The forms say the rental provider "must permit a fee-free (other than the renter's own bank fees) payment method and must allow the renter to use Centrepay or another form of electronic funds transfer." The renter is also "entitled to receive a receipt from the rental provider confirming payment of rent" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Your bond:** A rental provider who receives a bond must hold it on trust for the renter until it is paid to the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority (RTBA) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The provider must give the bond to the RTBA within 10 business days after receiving it, together with the completed bond lodgment form [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The RTBA must then send a receipt within 7 days [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). If you don't receive a receipt within 15 business days of paying the bond, you may notify the RTBA [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

### What to check before paying the new account

1. **Written notice of the change:** Ask for written confirmation that the owner is now managing the property and that the agent is no longer acting for them. Under the forms, the provider must notify you of changed details within 7 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
2. **Identity of the new account holder:** Confirm the account is in the owner's name (the rental provider named in your agreement). The documents don't address this, so it is general advice, not a legal requirement from these sources.
3. **Fee-free payment option:** Check that the owner offers a fee-free method other than cash, or Centrepay/electronic transfer, as the forms require [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Receipts:** Make sure you will receive a receipt for each rent payment [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
5. **Your bond:** Confirm the bond was lodged with the RTBA and that you received the bond lodgment form and the RTBA receipt [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). If you don't have the RTBA receipt, the documents say you may contact the RTBA (email rtba@justice.vic.gov.au or call 1300 137 164 per the form) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

### What the documents don't cover

- How to verify that bank details are genuine, or what to do if they look suspicious.
- Whether you can withhold rent or change how you pay if the owner doesn't give notice.
- Any rule about a change of owner ending the agency arrangement, or about the bond being transferred when management changes. The retrieved excerpts don't address this.

## What the law says

- **A free payment method must be available (s 42(4)).** The provider or agent must ensure a rent payment method with no additional costs is reasonably available to you. Bank fees or account fees on your own bank account don't count as additional costs. The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person and 400 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Your no-fee bank transfer may satisfy this. The Act doesn't say whether a slower method is still "reasonably available", so I can't say for certain.
- **Fees for electronic payment facilities are prohibited (s 51(3)).** A person must not demand or receive from a renter a charge for "the establishment or use of direct debit facilities or any other electronic payment facility for payment of rent". The penalty is 60 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). On its face this could cover a card fee in a rent app. The retrieved text doesn't say whether a card surcharge counts as an "electronic payment facility" charge, so I can't confirm that.
- **You must be told about costs first (s 42(7)).** The provider or agent must give you information about any costs you may incur by using a particular payment method. This includes third-party transaction fees and other electronic payment facility fees. They must do this before you consent to that method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

## Does it matter who gets the fee?

It may matter, but the documents leave a gap.

- **Section 51(3)** applies to "a person", so it isn't limited to agents. On its wording it could apply whether the fee goes to the app company or the agent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Section 51A** separately bans fees for a "prescribed matter" relating to the payment of rent. It applies to a person carrying on a business, but it excludes the residential rental provider, the provider's agent and authorised deposit-taking institutions (banks). An app company that isn't a bank would therefore be caught by s 51A if the fee relates to a prescribed matter [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The regulations that say what is "prescribed" weren't in the retrieved documents. I can't say whether a card fee is prescribed.

So the documents don't give a definite yes or no on the card fee. They also don't say how the answer changes depending on who receives the fee, beyond the points above.

## What you can do

- **Use the free method.** Pay by bank transfer, which has no fee. Section 42(4) is aimed at making sure that kind of option exists [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Ask for the costs in writing.** Ask the agent for the fee information required by s 42(7) before you agree to card payment [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Ask for a different payment arrangement.** You and the provider can agree to change how rent is paid (s 42(6)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Raise s 51(3) with the agent.** If you are being charged for using the app's payment facility, you can ask them to justify the charge under that section [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**1. Refuse to move in, and not pay rent until you do**
- A tenant isn't required to move into premises that fail the vacant and reasonably clean requirement [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- In that case you don't have to pay rent from the agreed move-in day until the day you actually move in [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- This protection is tied to "vacant and reasonably clean". Whether your mould and damp fit that is not answered in the documents.

**2. Ask for repairs**
- Give the landlord written notice of the damage and what it is. A tenant who becomes aware of damage must do this as soon as practicable [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Non-urgent repairs:**
  - If the landlord hasn't done the repairs within 14 days of your written notice, you can apply in writing to the Director to investigate [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
  - You can then apply to the Tribunal within 60 days of receiving the Director's report. You can also apply if you haven't received the report within 90 days of asking for it [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
  - The Tribunal can order specified repairs and set a deadline [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs:**
  - If you've taken reasonable steps to get the landlord to act immediately and can't, you may arrange the repairs yourself. You must give 14 days' written notice of the work and its cost [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
  - The landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost, up to $1000 [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
  - If you can't meet the cost, the repairs cost more than $1000, or the landlord refuses to pay, you can apply to the Tribunal. It must hear the application within 2 business days [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Gap in the documents:** the v088 definition of "urgent repairs" wasn't in the retrieved text. The explicit "mould or damp" wording I found appears only in later versions and in the amending-Act endnotes, so I can't confirm it applied in October 2019.

**3. Pay rent into the Rent Special Account**
- After you've given notice requiring repairs, you can apply to the Tribunal to pay your rent into the Rent Special Account if the landlord hasn't done them [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- This holds the rent. It does not reduce it. The landlord can apply for it to be released if repairs are being done [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**4. Lower rent**
- The retrieved text of s 47 lets the Tribunal consider whether rent is more than a tenant should reasonably pay. It looks at factors including "the state of repair and general condition of the rented premises" [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- If it makes such an order, the landlord can't require more than the ordered rent for 12 months. The Tribunal can also order a refund of the difference [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- The start of s 47 and the rules on who can apply and when weren't in the retrieved text, so I can't say how that process works for a tenant who hasn't yet moved in.

**5. Cancel the lease**
- A tenant may give notice of intention to vacate if the premises are "unfit for human habitation" or have been destroyed or made unsafe. The termination date can be the date of the notice or later [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- Whether your damp, mould and rotting timber meet "unfit for human habitation" is not answered in the documents.
- An ordinary notice of intention to vacate must give at least 28 days. For a fixed-term lease it has no effect if the termination date is before the end of the term [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

The documents don't say whether any lease-break cost applies if you cancel.

**In practice:** put the defects in writing to the landlord or agent now, with photos. That starts the repair process, and the Director and Tribunal steps above depend on written notice.

## What the law says

The *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* version in force is `rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf` (version 005, in force 25 Nov 2025 to 9 Feb 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

- **Smoke alarm duty.** Under s 68AA of version 111, the rental provider must make sure each smoke alarm is correctly installed and working. It must have batteries, and it must be tested at least once every 12 months in line with the manufacturer's instructions [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). If the alarm is mains-powered, a suitably qualified person must do the testing, repair or replacement [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Entry.** The Regulations (version 005) include a standard-form summary of entry rights. It says the renter "must allow entry to the premises where the rental provider has followed proper procedure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- **Gap in the documents.** The version 111 text I retrieved doesn't include the entry provisions (ss 85–89). Those sections appear only in other versions I retrieved:
  - Version 101 (dated 7 Sept 2022) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)
  - Version 115 (dated 13 Oct 2026, which is after today's date and so not yet in force) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
  
  I can't confirm that either matches the wording in force today.

**For indication only, from the 2022 version (v101) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf):**
- Entry to carry out the provider's duty needs at least 24 hours' written notice. It must be between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. on a day that isn't a public holiday.
- Alternatively, entry can be at a time you agreed to, if you consented within the 7 days before.
- You have a duty to permit lawful entry. You can apply to the Tribunal for an order limiting when entry may occur.

None of the retrieved versions say the renter must be present. They also don't mention a 10 am–12:30 pm window or any fee for rebooking.

## Your two questions

1. **Do you have to be home?** The documents don't say so. They say you must allow entry when proper procedure is followed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). I found no provision requiring you to be there in person.
2. **Can they charge $90?** I found nothing in the retrieved documents that authorises a rebooking fee, and nothing that prohibits one. I can't say either way.

## What you can do

- Ask the agent in writing which section of the Act or which lease term supports both the "must be home" requirement and the $90 fee.
- Check that you received a proper written entry notice stating the reason for entry [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

I've used the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 101** (file "rta-1997-v101-2022-09-07.pdf", in force 7 September 2022 to 23 May 2023). That was the version in force on 8 November 2022. I've also used the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, version 002** (file "rt-regs-2021-v002-2022-06-01.pdf", in force from 1 June 2022).

- **Where and how rent is paid:** Rent is payable at the place specified in the agreement, or at the rented premises if none is specified. It is payable in the manner (if any) specified in the agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The agreement form has a "payment details" field for the rental provider's payment methods [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Changes need agreement:** The rental provider and renter "by agreement" may change how rent is payable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The documents don't say a renter must accept a new account that the renter hasn't agreed to. That follows from the "by agreement" wording, and the documents don't state it outright.
- **Costs and a fee-free option:** The rental provider or their agent must make a payment method with no extra costs available. Your own bank fees don't count as extra costs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). They must also tell you about any costs of a particular payment method before you consent to it, including third-party transaction fees and other electronic payment fees [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). They must allow Centrepay and any prescribed payment method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Receipts:** Whoever receives your rent must give a written receipt immediately if you pay in person. If you don't pay in person, they must give one within 5 business days of receiving the payment if you ask for it when you pay. The receipt must state your name and the premises, the date, the period paid, the amount, and that it is for rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). If a receipt isn't required, they must still keep a record of the payment for 12 months. If you ask for a copy, they must give it to you within 5 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Change of agent or owner details:** The standard agreement form says the rental provider must notify the renter within 7 days if the rental provider or agent details change [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The form also says the parties must immediately notify each other in writing if their contact details change [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The Act section that requires written notice of changes (s 66(4)) appears only in a later version, Version 115 (in force 13 October 2026) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). That version is after your date, so I can't treat it as the law on 8 November 2022. The retrieved text of Version 101 doesn't include that section.

## What you can check or ask for

1. **Get the change in writing from the owner.** Ask for written confirmation of the owner's full name and address for service, and their contact details. The standard form expects to be notified of these changes [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
2. **Check your agreement.** See what it says about the place and manner of payment, and the "payment details" in the payment methods section [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). If the new account differs, ask for the change to be recorded as an agreed change [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
3. **Confirm through a channel you already trust.** Phone the agency on the number in your agreement, and contact the owner using details you can verify. The retrieved documents say nothing specific about payment-redirection scams, so this is a common-sense step and not a legal requirement.
4. **Ask about costs.** Ask whether the new method has any fees, and whether a fee-free method is available [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
5. **Ask for receipts.** Request a written receipt each time you pay. Under the Act, they must give you one within 5 business days if you request it when you pay by transfer [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
6. **Check your bond.** Your bond should be lodged with the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority within 10 business days of payment. If you haven't received the Authority's receipt within 15 business days, the form says to email rtba@justice.vic.gov.au or call 1300 137 164 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

The retrieved documents don't cover how an owner takes over from an agent mid-lease, or what happens to money already paid to the agency. Consumer Affairs Victoria could help with those questions.

## What the law says — 15 January 2026

The applicable documents are:

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 111**, in force from **25 November 2025** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 005**, in force from **25 November 2025** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

The rental provider or agent must ensure that you have a rent-payment method that incurs **no additional cost**, apart from bank or account fees payable on your own bank account, and that method must be **reasonably available**. A fee-free manual bank transfer appears capable of satisfying that requirement, even if paying by card is faster. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

The provider or agent must also tell you about costs you may incur with a particular payment method—including third-party transaction fees and electronic-payment-facility fees—**before you consent to use it**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

As at 15 January 2026, the retrieved regulations do **not** prescribe the specific rent-payment fees covered by the newer prohibition in section 51A. Therefore, these documents do not establish that the card fee is automatically prohibited under section 51A on that date. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The Act separately prohibits a person from charging for the **establishment or use of an electronic payment facility** for paying rent. However, the retrieved documents do not explain whether this particular card surcharge is such a charge, or whether the app company is legally acting as the rental provider’s agent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

It does not necessarily matter that the fee goes to the app company rather than the agent: section 51(3) applies to **“a person.”** But the retrieved documents do not provide enough information to determine whether that provision applies to this particular app fee. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

You can:

1. **Use or request the fee-free bank-transfer option**, provided it is reasonably available. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
2. Ask the agent or rental provider to confirm in writing:
   - the amount and nature of the card fee;
   - who receives it—the app company, agent or someone else; and
   - why they say it is legally chargeable.
3. Ask for the required information about all costs before consenting to use the card-payment method. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

On these documents alone, the clearest conclusion is: **the app must leave you a reasonably available fee-free rent-payment method, but the documents do not conclusively determine whether the separate card fee itself is lawful, nor whether its recipient changes that result.**

## What the law says

On **15 October 2019**, the applicable document was **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 088**, incorporating amendments as at **2 July 2019**. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

Because you had **not yet entered into possession**, section 226 allowed you to terminate the tenancy by giving the landlord a notice of termination if the premises:

- were **not in good repair**;
- were **unfit for human habitation**;
- were unsafe;
- were not legally available or otherwise unavailable for occupation. [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

The landlord also had a duty to maintain the premises in **good repair**. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) The Act treated a fault or damage making premises unsafe or insecure as an **urgent repair**, including mould or damp caused by, or related to, the building structure. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

1. **Cancel/terminate before moving in:**  
   Give the landlord written notice under **section 226**, stating that you have not entered possession and that the premises are not in good repair, are unfit for habitation, or are otherwise unavailable for occupation. [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) The documents do not state that merely receiving the keys prevents you using section 226; the stated condition is that you have **not entered into possession**. [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

2. **Ask for repairs:**  
   Notify the landlord in writing and request immediate repairs. If the mould or damp is structural and makes the premises unsafe or insecure, it may be an urgent repair. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) If the landlord does not act, you may arrange urgent repairs after taking reasonable steps to get the landlord or agent to do them; the landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost or **$1,000, whichever is less**, after you give **14 days’ written notice** of the repairs and cost. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) You may instead apply to the Tribunal for urgent-repair orders if you cannot meet the cost, the repairs exceed $1,000, or the landlord refuses to pay; the Tribunal must hear that application within **2 business days**. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

   For non-urgent repairs, give written notice. If they are not done within **14 days**, you may ask the Director to investigate and then apply to the Tribunal for a repair order. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

3. **Ask for lower rent:**  
   The retrieved documents do **not** provide a general right, on these facts, to unilaterally reduce the rent. They do provide a process to apply to the Tribunal for permission to pay rent into the **Rent Special Account** after notice requiring repairs has been given and the landlord has failed to comply. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) Do not simply stop paying rent without an order.

If you aren't given one, you may complete one yourself and give it to the provider before 5 business days after you move in [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A condition report you give the provider is taken as notice of any defects it states [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do

1. **Put it in writing now.** You must give written notice "as soon as practicable after becoming aware of" damage [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). List the damp, mould and rotting timber, and record them on the condition report.
2. **Ask for repairs.** For urgent repairs, you may arrange them yourself if you have taken reasonable steps to get the provider to do them immediately and they haven't [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You must give the provider 7 days' written notice of the repairs and cost [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations summary says this is directly reimbursable "up to $2500" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Non-urgent repairs:** If repairs are not urgent, you must give written notice, and you can apply to the Director if the provider hasn't repaired within 14 days [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You can apply to VCAT for an order requiring repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). VCAT must hear a non-urgent repair application within 7 days of it being made [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Urgent-repair applications:** You can apply to VCAT for an order requiring urgent repairs if you cannot meet the cost, the cost is more than $2500, or the provider refuses to pay [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). VCAT must hear these within 2 business days [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. **Pay rent into the Rent Special Account:** If you have given notice requiring repairs, you may apply to VCAT for an order to pay rent into the Rent Special Account [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). VCAT must make that order if the provider has failed to carry out the repairs and has not shown financial hardship [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
6. **Amend the condition report:** Within 30 days after the agreement starts, you may apply to VCAT to amend a statement in the condition report that is inaccurate or incomplete [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

- **Cancelling:** The Regulations' standard form refers to a renter giving notice of intention to vacate under "section 91ZD" where premises are "destroyed or unfit for habitation" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). **What the law says**

- "Urgent repairs" includes a failure or breakdown of the water supply to rented premises, and a failure or breakdown of an essential water service or fitting provided by the landlord [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Whether a broken tap alone qualifies is a judgement call. The documents don't say, but a whole-house water shut-off is a strong case for urgency. Consumer Affairs Victoria's urgent repairs guidance is referred to in the Regulations [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, both urgent and non-urgent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The Act defines a suitably qualified person to include a registered or licensed tradesperson where the work requires licensing [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). So you can't do the plumbing yourself. You can engage a suitably qualified person.

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Notify the owner in writing now.** Renters should notify the landlord in writing as soon as practicable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Use the emergency contact details in your agreement [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Record that the owner's tradespeople can't attend yet.
2. **Arrange a suitably qualified person** if the owner still can't act promptly [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Keep records of the steps you took to reach the owner.
3. **Give written notice of the repairs and their cost within 7 days** of the work being done [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Ask for reimbursement.** The landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost, or the prescribed amount if that is less [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations state that a renter may be reimbursed for reasonable repair costs up to $2,500 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The owner must reimburse within 7 days after receiving your written notice of the repairs and cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. **If the owner refuses to pay or you can't meet the cost,** you may apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT). The Tribunal must hear an urgent repair application within 2 business days of it being made [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**Gaps in the documents:** They don't say how a court or VCAT would treat a broken tap specifically, and they don't set out a fixed time for "immediately" beyond the reasonable-steps test. Check with Consumer Affairs Victoria before acting.

These are the versions identified in the retrieved metadata.

### What the law says

- **Professional cleaning clauses are limited.** The prescribed wording says the provider "must not require the renter to arrange professional cleaning or cleaning to a professional standard at the end of the tenancy" unless either the premises were professionally cleaned before the tenancy started and the renter was told so, or professional cleaning "is required to restore the rented premises to the same condition they were in immediately before the start of the tenancy, having regard to the condition report and taking into account fair wear and tear" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **The renter's obligation is conditional.** The renter must have the premises professionally cleaned, or pay for it, only "if professional cleaning becomes required" under that same test [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Non-standard terms can be invalid.** A residential rental agreement must not include a term requiring professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy "unless that term is contained in the standard form" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). An invalid term is void [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and the Tribunal can declare a term invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The end-of-lease standard.** At the end, a renter must leave the premises "as far as practicable" reasonably clean and "in the same condition as when the renter entered into possession... taking into account fair wear and tear" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Bond deductions.** A landlord may claim the reasonable cost of cleaning only "if the premises were not left reasonably clean by the renter, having regard to the condition of the premises at the commencement" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do or ask

1. **Ask whether professional cleaning is actually required.** Under the test above, the question is whether carpets that you've cleaned are back to their move-in condition, allowing for fair wear and tear. If they are, the clause's condition for a professional clean isn't met [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
2. **Check the clause wording against the standard form.** If your lease's cleaning term differs from the prescribed wording, it may be invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Gather evidence of the carpets' condition:**
   - **Your move-in condition report.** The renter should fill in the report within 5 business days after moving in, and it "may help the renter verify the condition... if there is a later dispute about the renter's responsibility for damage or cleaning" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Note any carpet issues you disagreed with.
   - **Dated photos.** The condition report guidance says photos "should be taken at the beginning and at the end of the tenancy," and should be dated and labelled by location [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
   - **The end-of-lease condition report.** The provider must complete it "within 10 days after the end date" and give the renter an opportunity to attend if possible [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Check that it describes the carpets accurately, and if not, record your disagreement and attach your photos [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
4. **Respond in writing.** If you disagree with any statement, you can record that disagreement on your copy of the report. A signed condition report is conclusive evidence of the premises' state of repair or general condition on the stated day, subject to exceptions [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Note that this covers repair or general condition, not necessarily cleaning.
5. **Watch for a bond claim.** Before the provider claims cleaning costs from your bond, they must give you "bond claim evidence" at least 3 days before the claim is made, and that evidence "must not conflict with a statement in a condition report" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What the documents don't cover

- **The receipt requirement.** The documents don't say a renter must provide a professional cleaner's receipt, or that a self-clean is insufficient as proof.
- **What counts as "required."** The documents don't define when a professional clean is "required" beyond the restore-to-move-in-condition test.
- **Your specific lease.** I don't have your lease, so I can't tell whether its clause uses the standard-form wording.

If the agent insists and you can't resolve it, the documents mention VCAT as the forum for disputes over bond claims and condition reports [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), but they don't set out the full process here. For specific advice, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria.

You must give 7 days' written notice of the repairs and their cost. - **Non-urgent repairs.** Give written notice. If the provider hasn't acted within 14 days, you can ask the Director to investigate or apply to VCAT [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). VCAT must hear that application within 7 days [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).   - Professional cleaning is needed to restore the premises to the same condition they were in at the start, "having regard to the condition report and taking into account fair wear and tear".
- You must have premises professionally cleaned, or pay for it, only if that cleaning becomes required to restore them to their starting condition, again having regard to the condition report and fair wear and tear [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

If the carpets really are back to their starting condition, professional cleaning isn't "required" under the standard term [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
