The obligations apply to the residential rental provider or the provider’s agent, and the separate prohibition applies to a “person”; however, the retrieved documents do not determine the app company’s legal status or whether it is an ADI. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The Tribunal may order repairs by a suitably qualified person and compensation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Based on the current Victorian residential tenancy laws:

**What the law says**
Under Victorian residential tenancy law, your rental provider or their agent has two main obligations regarding how you pay rent:
1. **A fee-free option must be available:** They must ensure that a rent payment method with no additional costs (other than your own bank's standard fees) is reasonably available to you [Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (v115, 13 Oct 2026)] [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Since your app offers a manual bank transfer with no fee, this requirement is met [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Costs must be disclosed upfront:** Before you agree to use a specific payment method, the provider or agent must tell you about any costs you might incur, which explicitly includes "third party transaction fees" and other electronic payment facility fees [Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (v115, 13 Oct 2026)] [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 

Regarding whether the app can charge the fee: The law prohibits landlords and agents from charging you for the *establishment or use* of direct debit or other electronic payment facilities [Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (v009, 30 Jun 2026)] [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). However, it explicitly acknowledges that third-party transaction fees (like card processing fees charged by an external app) may apply, provided they are disclosed beforehand [Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (v115, 13 Oct 2026)] [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 

Does it matter who receives the fee? The law places the legal responsibility on the **residential rental provider or their agent** to provide a free payment method and disclose any costs, regardless of whether a third-party app collects the fee [Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (v115, 13 Oct 2026)] [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If your agent is directly demanding or pocketing the card fee themselves, they are likely breaching the rule against charging for the use of electronic payment facilities [Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (v009, 30 Jun 2026)] [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). If the fee goes to an independent app company as a processing charge, it is permissible only if you were informed of it before consenting to use that method [Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (v115, 13 Oct 2026)] [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask**
- **Use the free option:** You are fully entitled to pay via the manual bank transfer without penalty. 
- **Ask for disclosure:** If you haven't already been told about the card fee, ask your agent in writing: *"Please confirm in writing what third-party transaction fees apply if I choose to pay by card, as required under section 42(7) of the Residential Tenancies Act 1997."* [Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (v115, 13 Oct 2026)] [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- **Check who is charging you:** If your agent is adding the fee directly to your rent invoice rather than it being a separate charge from the payment app itself, this may be an illegal charge for using an electronic payment facility [Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (v009, 30 Jun 2026)] [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). 
- **Lodge a complaint:** If the provider or agent refuses to offer a fee-free method, fails to disclose third-party fees, or illegally charges you for using electronic payments, you can lodge a complaint with Consumer Affairs Victoria or apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) [Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (v115, 13 Oct 2026)] [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**Yes.** Because you have not yet moved in, the Act provides a specific provision for **"Termination by renter before possession"** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Since the property fails to meet the mandatory rental minimum standards (structural soundness and freedom from building-related damp/mould) and is not in a fit condition for occupation, you can terminate the agreement before taking possession.

### 3. Can you ask for repairs?
**Yes.** You must notify the landlord of the damage **in writing as soon as practicable** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
- **Urgent Repairs:** If the damp, mould, or rotting timber poses an immediate health or safety risk, it qualifies as an urgent repair. The landlord must carry out these repairs immediately upon being notified [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Non-Urgent Repairs:** For other maintenance issues, the landlord must complete them within a reasonable time. If they fail to do so within **14 days** of receiving your written notice, you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring the landlord to carry out the repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### 4. Can you ask for lower rent?
You **cannot unilaterally reduce your rent** on your own. However, if the landlord fails to fix the issues, you have two legal avenues regarding rent:
- **Rent Special Account:** You can apply to VCAT to pay your rent into a "Rent Special Account" instead of paying the landlord directly while the repairs are pending [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
- **Compensation:** If VCAT finds that the landlord breached their duty to maintain the premises, they can order the landlord to pay you compensation for the breach [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### Recommended Next Steps
1. Document the damp, mould, and rotting timber with photos/videos.
2. Send a written notice to your landlord/agent detailing the issues and requesting repairs (or termination before possession).
3. If they refuse or delay, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria or apply to VCAT for urgent orders.

You do **not** have to wait. You are legally permitted to arrange for a suitably qualified person to fix the issue yourself, provided you follow these steps:

### What the Law Says
Under Victorian tenancy law, a rental provider **cannot** demand professional cleaning or a receipt from a professional cleaner unless it is actually necessary to restore the property to the condition it was in when you moved in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The standard form agreement only permits a requirement for professional cleaning if:
* Professional cleaning was carried out immediately before your tenancy started and you were advised of this; **or**
* Professional cleaning is required to restore the premises to their original condition, having regard to the condition report and taking into account fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

Additionally, at the end of a tenancy, you are legally required to leave the rented premises "reasonably clean" and in the same condition as when you entered, accounting for fair wear and tear [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If your DIY cleaning has already returned the carpets to their original state (minus fair wear and tear), you have fulfilled this legal duty.

### What You Can Do or Ask
* **You do not have to pay for a professional cleaner** if the carpets are already back to how they were when you moved in. The agent's blanket demand for a receipt is unenforceable because the standard has already been met [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
* **Ask the agent to review your condition report and photos** as proof that the cleaning standard was satisfied, rather than insisting on a professional receipt. If they attempt to deduct money from your bond for this, you can formally dispute the claim using your move-in/move-out evidence [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What Helps Show the Carpets' Condition
To prove you left the carpets in the required condition, rely on these two documents:
1. **The Condition Report:** You are entitled to receive 2 copies (or 1 emailed copy) of a condition report on or before your move-in date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). You must fill yours out within 5 business days of moving in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). This document records the state of the floor coverings at the start of your tenancy. At the end of the lease, the agent must complete the final inspection section within 10 days and allow for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Comparing your move-in report to the move-out report is the primary way to prove the carpets were left in the same condition.
2. **Dated Photos:** You should take photos at both the beginning and end of your tenancy showing the condition of the floor coverings [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The law advises taking close-up photos to show detail, as well as wider shots for perspective [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Ensure these photos are dated, labelled with the room/location, and attached to your copy of the condition report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). These visual records are explicitly noted as being useful in resolving disputes about the condition of the rented premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### What the Law Says About Your Situation
Under Victorian tenancy law, a residential rental provider has a duty to ensure the rented premises are maintained in good repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Crucially, the law distinguishes between damage caused by tenants and damage caused by third parties. A landlord is only entitled to issue a notice to vacate for serious damage if *you* or your visitor intentionally or recklessly caused it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Because the damage was caused by burglars during break-ins, this provision does not apply against you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What You Can Do Before Your Lease Ends
You have three primary legal options to address the damage and protect your tenancy:

**1. Report the Damage Immediately**
You are legally required to notify your landlord as soon as practicable after becoming aware of the damage or breakdown of facilities, fixtures, furniture, or equipment [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This written notice must clearly state both the fact that the damage occurred and its nature . 

**2. Get Urgent Repairs Done (Plumbing & Wiring)**
Damaged plumbing and wiring likely qualify as urgent repairs. You have two pathways to get them fixed:
* **Arrange the repairs yourself:** If you have taken reasonable steps to get your landlord or their agent to immediately carry out the repairs but are unable to get them to do so, you may arrange for urgent repairs yourself [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You must give your landlord 7 days' written notice of the repairs carried out and the cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The landlord is liable to reimburse you for the reasonable cost (up to a prescribed amount) within 7 days after receiving your notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* **Apply to the Tribunal:** If you cannot meet the cost of the repairs, if the repairs cost more than the prescribed amount, or if your landlord refuses to pay, you can apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring them to carry out the urgent repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Tribunal must hear this application within 2 business days after it is made [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**3. Terminate the Lease Early (If the Property is Uninhabitable)**
If the damage from the break-ins is severe enough that your home is no longer safe or livable, you can end the lease early without penalty:
* Under section 91ZD, if the premises are "unfit for human habitation" or have been destroyed totally or to such an extent as to be "rendered unsafe," you may give your landlord a notice of intention to vacate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
* This notice can specify a termination date that is the same day you give it, or a later date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* Terminating under this section means you are not liable to pay any form of lease break fee [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

*Note: While the retrieved documents outline your rights to report damage, claim urgent repair costs, and terminate the lease if the property is unsafe, they do not explicitly detail the process for claiming compensation from burglars' insurance or bond adjustments for third-party criminal damage. You may wish to consult Consumer Affairs Victoria or a legal aid service for guidance on those specific financial recovery steps.*

- **Duty to repair:** The landlord (residential rental provider) must maintain the premises in good repair [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Before you move in:** An older version of the Act (2020) said a tenant is not required to move in if the premises don't comply with the landlord's duty to be vacant and reasonably clean, and no rent is payable until the tenant actually moves in [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf). The current excerpts I retrieved don't include this provision, so please check it in the current Act before relying on it.

## What you can do or ask

**1. Ask for repairs in writing (required first step).** You must give the provider written notice "as soon as practicable" after becoming aware of damage [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**2. Urgent repairs.** If the problem is urgent, you may arrange repairs if you have taken reasonable steps to get the provider to do them immediately and they haven't. You must give 7 days' written notice of the repairs and cost, and the provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days of that notice [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A 2025 version of the standard form summarised the cap as $2,500 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). That is not the current figure, so verify it. If you can't afford the repairs, or the provider refuses to pay, you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring repairs [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). VCAT must hear an urgent repair application within 2 business days [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**3. Non-urgent repairs.** If you give written notice and the provider doesn't carry out the repairs within 14 days, you can apply to the Director to investigate [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) or apply to VCAT [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). VCAT must hear a non-urgent repair application within 7 days [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). VCAT can order specified repairs, use of a suitably qualified person, and compensation [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**4. Rent.** If you have given notice requiring repairs, you can apply to VCAT to pay your rent into the Rent Special Account [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This holds the rent rather than reducing it. VCAT can order the rent paid to you if the required repairs are not done by the deadline in its order [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). **The documents do not contain a power to reduce rent.**

**5. Cancelling the lease.** **The retrieved documents do not cover this.** I can't say whether you can cancel based on these defects.

**6. Condition report.** Your condition report is a record of the premises' state at the start. A 2025 version of the regulations' Form 4 said that if you later find something not working or in poor repair, you may apply to VCAT to correct the report within 30 days after the start date of the agreement [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The current Form 4 is not in the retrieved excerpts, so check it.

---

**Next steps:** Document everything with dated photos, put your complaint in writing, and check the current Act and regulations on the Consumer Affairs Victoria website, or get advice from a tenants' legal service before deciding whether to end the lease.

answer:
**Short answer:** You don't have to wait indefinitely. If you've taken reasonable steps to get the landlord or agent to do the repair immediately and they cannot, the law lets you arrange urgent repairs yourself. The owner's restriction to their own tradespeople doesn't settle the question, and the documents don't say whether it does.

**Which documents I relied on:** The current Regulations are *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, version 009, in force from 30 June 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The Act text I found is *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, version 111, which is in force from 25 November 2025 to 29 June 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Nothing I retrieved covers the Act from 30 June 2026 onward, so I can't confirm that version is still the current one. Section 72 has the same wording in version 110 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), and I'm relying on version 111.

**What the law says**

- A renter may arrange urgent repairs if they have taken reasonable steps to get the landlord or agent to carry them out immediately, and they are unable to get the landlord or agent to do them [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- A burst water service is given as an example of an urgent repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, both urgent and non-urgent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). So any plumber you engage should be properly qualified.

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Report it in writing now.** Give the landlord or agent written notice as soon as practicable [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The emergency contact on the form is the person to use for urgent repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
2. **Keep a record of every attempt** to get the repair done immediately, including the time, who you contacted, and their response. This evidence supports the "reasonable steps" and "unable to get" requirements [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
3. **If they still can't attend, arrange a suitably qualified person** to fix it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
4. **Give written notice afterwards.** Within 7 days you must give the landlord written notice of the repairs and their cost [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
5. **Ask for reimbursement.** The landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost, or the prescribed amount if that is less, and must pay within 7 days of receiving your written notice [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The Regulations state that you may be reimbursed directly for the reasonable cost of repairs up to $2500 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
6. **If the landlord refuses to pay or the cost is too high, go to VCAT.** You can apply if you cannot meet the cost, the repairs cost more than $2500, or the landlord refuses to pay [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The Tribunal must hear an urgent repair application within 2 business days of it being made [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover:** They don't say whether a landlord can require their own tradespeople, or how long the landlord has to respond before you can act. They also don't address the effect of shutting off the water to the whole house. If you're unsure, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria (consumer.vic.gov.au/urgentrepairs), which the Regulations refer to for the full list of urgent repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**Short answer:** Probably not, if the carpets are back to their move-in condition. The rules turn on whether professional cleaning is *required* to restore the premises, not on whether the lease clause mentions it. The documents don't say the agent can insist on a professional's receipt.

**Which document applies:** The current document is the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (S.R. No. 3/2021), Authorised Version **009**, which has effect from 30 June 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The Act itself ([Residential Tenancies Act 1997](#)) has no current version in these results. The latest Act text I found, version 110, was in force only until 24 November 2025 [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), so I can't confirm the current Act wording.

### What the law says

- **Landlord's limit:** The landlord "must not require the renter to arrange professional cleaning or cleaning to a professional standard at the end of the tenancy" unless either (a) professional cleaning was done before the tenancy started and the renter was told so, or (b) professional cleaning "is required to restore the rented premises to the same condition they were in immediately before the start of the tenancy, having regard to the condition report and taking into account fair wear and tear" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Renter's obligation:** The renter must pay for or arrange professional cleaning only "if professional cleaning becomes required to restore the premises to the condition they were in immediately before the start of the tenancy" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The standard-form wording (Form 1, item 11) says the same [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Renter's general duty:** At the end of the agreement, the renter must leave the premises "as far as practicable" reasonably clean and in the same condition as when they moved in, taking into account fair wear and tear [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa098%20authorised.pdf). This is from a 2021 version of the Act, so check it against the current text.
- **Clause validity:** The Act says a landlord must not include a term requiring professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy "unless that term is contained in the standard form" [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). A term that is not in the standard form may be invalid, and a renter can apply to the Tribunal for an order declaring a term invalid or varying it [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do or ask

1. **Compare the carpets to the condition report.** The cleaning test refers to the condition report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). If the agent's report describes the carpets as clean at move-in, your evidence that they are now in that state matters most.
2. **Ask the agent to say why professional cleaning is required.** Under the regulation, the requirement must be one needed to restore the original condition, taking into account fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Ask them to identify what is still not restored.
3. **Gather your own evidence.** The documents don't list what evidence is acceptable. Practical options (my suggestions, not from the documents) include dated photos and video of each room, your cleaning receipts for products, and the move-in condition report.
4. **Consider the Tribunal if it stays unresolved.** If the agent insists and you disagree, the Act allows an application to the Tribunal [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The documents don't give the process or costs, so check with the Tribunal or Consumer Affairs Victoria.

**Not covered by the documents:** whether a professional receipt is required as proof, what counts as acceptable evidence, and how the bond process handles disputed cleaning. The regulations don't address these points.

The renter must then give the landlord 7 days' written notice of the repairs and the cost. The landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days of receiving that notice, up to the prescribed amount [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). It includes "a dangerous electrical fault", "a burst water service", "a blocked or broken lavatory system", and "any fault or damage that makes rented premises unsafe or insecure" [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf). The current definition wasn't in the retrieved text, so please confirm it before relying on it.
- **Cleaning at the end:** A renter must leave the premises "as far as practicable" reasonably clean and in the same condition as when they moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The "as far as practicable" wording may matter here, but the documents don't address damage that prevents cleaning.
- **Renter's damage duty:** A renter and any visitor must not intentionally or negligently damage the premises, and fair wear and tear is excluded [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether burglars count as "visitors." The definition of visitor refers to a person on the premises "with the permission of the tenant" [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf), which suggests they would not, but this is my inference, not something the documents state.

## What you can do or ask

1. **Give written notice now** to the landlord describing the break-ins and the damaged plumbing and wiring [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**Governing version:** Today is 5 November 2026, and the Act version in force is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What the law says

- **Cleaning can be claimed from the bond.** A landlord may claim "the reasonable cost of cleaning any part of the premises, if the premises were not left reasonably clean by the renter, having regard to the condition of the premises at the commencement of the residential rental agreement" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Evidence must be provided first.** At least 3 days before a claim to the provider is made, the provider or their agent "must give each renter bond claim evidence that supports the claim" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Bond claim evidence means an invoice, receipt, quote, photograph, or other prescribed evidence [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The evidence must match the condition report.** Bond claim evidence "must not conflict with a statement in a condition report" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Your duty to leave the premises clean.** At the end of a tenancy, a renter must leave the premises "as far as practicable" reasonably clean [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The text I retrieved for this section is from Version 110, which is no longer in force, so I could not confirm the current wording in Version 115.

### What you can do or ask

1. **Ask for the bond claim evidence.** Ask whether the agent gave you an invoice, receipt, quote or photographs at least 3 days before the claim, and check whether it conflicts with your condition report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Check what the claim was for.** Cleaning is only claimable if the premises were not left reasonably clean, judged against their condition at the start of the tenancy [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Ask the Authority about any other party's claim.** If a claim is made without everyone's consent, the Authority must notify the other parties, who have 14 days to say the claim is subject to a Tribunal application [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Apply to the Tribunal if you dispute it.** An application for a bond repayment order "must be made within 14 days after the residential rental agreement has terminated" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What the documents don't cover

- Whether agreeing to a bond deduction is the same as agreeing to pay an invoice. The retrieved sections don't address this.
- Whether an agent can send a separate invoice after the bond has been fully refunded.
- Whether your earlier agreement was valid or binding, or what effect it had.

For these points, you'd need the residential tenancy agreement, any written deduction agreement, and advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria or the Tribunal (VCAT).

3. **Go to VCAT (the Tribunal) for urgent repairs.** You can apply for an order that the provider carry out specified urgent repairs if:
   - you can't meet the cost;
   - the cost is over the prescribed amount ($2500 per the standard agreement); or
   - the provider refuses to pay [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

   The Tribunal must hear the application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Non-urgent repairs.** Give written notice. If the provider hasn't acted within 14 days, you can apply to the Director to investigate or apply to the Tribunal for an order. The Tribunal must hear that application within 7 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). It must consider whether the repairs are needed because of the renter's act or omission, and whether the provider was notified and had a reasonable opportunity to act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. **Pay rent into the Rent Special Account.** After giving repair notice, you can ask the Tribunal to authorise this. It must do so if the provider has failed to do the repairs and hasn't shown financial hardship [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
6. **Locks.** If the provider withholds consent to a lock change and you think that's unreasonable, you can ask the Tribunal to decide that consent isn't required [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

- **Bond claims go through the Bond Authority.** A claim can be made jointly by provider and renter for repayment of the bond to the renter, to the provider, or split between them (s 411(1)(c)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Authority must repay the bond where the claim is made jointly under that provision (s 411AC(a)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Evidence must come first.** At least 3 days before a claim for repayment of bond to the provider, the provider or agent must give each renter "bond claim evidence". That means an invoice, receipt, quote, photograph or other prescribed evidence (ss 411(1A), 3(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The evidence must not conflict with a statement in a condition report (s 411(1B)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Signing a claim form.** A provider must not request or obtain your signature on a claim form that doesn't specify the amount of bond to be refunded and how it is apportioned (s 411(5)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Professional cleaning.** The prescribed regulation says a provider must not require professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy unless:
  - the premises were professionally cleaned just before the tenancy started and you were told so; or
  - professional cleaning is needed to restore the premises to their starting condition, having regard to the condition report and fair wear and tear [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Who pays for professional cleaning.** The prescribed term lets the renter be made to pay for professional cleaning only if it becomes required to restore the premises to that starting condition [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic)** (version 111, in force from 25 November 2025) and the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (Vic)** (version 005, in force from 25 November 2025), here is how the law applies to your situation:

### Can the app charge you a card fee?
Third-party apps are generally permitted to charge processing fees for card payments, which the law classifies as **"third party transaction fees"** or **"electronic payment facility fees"** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). However, the rental provider or their agent **cannot force you to use a paid method** if a free alternative exists. They must ensure that a rent payment method with **no additional costs** (other than your own bank's account/transaction fees) is reasonably available to you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). 

### Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or the agent?
**No, it does not matter.** The law focuses entirely on the cost *to you, the renter*. 
* The rental provider or agent is legally required to permit at least one **fee-free payment method** (such as direct debit or bank deposit) regardless of who collects the fee for the paid option [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 
* Whether the card fee is retained by the app company or passed through to the agent does not change the provider's legal duty to offer you a free alternative [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do
1. **Use the free option:** You are fully entitled to use the manual bank transfer (or other fee-free methods like Centrepay) without penalty [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 
2. **Verify disclosure:** The provider or agent must explicitly inform you of any costs you might incur before you consent to use a specific payment method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). If they haven't, they have breached their legal duty.
3. **Demand a free alternative:** If the app makes the card fee mandatory because no other payment methods are offered, the rental provider or agent is breaking the law by failing to ensure a fee-free method is reasonably available [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

*(Note: These rules apply to standard residential tenancies in Victoria. Different provisions may apply if your landlord is Homes Victoria [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).)*

### What the law says
A broken tap that cuts off water to the entire house qualifies as an **urgent repair** [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The rental provider (owner) has a strict legal duty to carry out urgent repairs immediately after being notified [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). You **do not** have to wait. You can take the following steps:
1. **Confirm you've taken reasonable steps:** Ensure you have clearly notified the owner/agent of the urgent repair and given them a chance to arrange it immediately [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). 
2. **Arrange the repair yourself:** If the owner still hasn't fixed it, you are entitled to hire a suitably qualified tradesperson to carry out the urgent repairs [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Claim reimbursement:** The owner is legally required to reimburse you for the reasonable cost of these repairs, up to a maximum of **$2500** [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Keep all invoices and receipts to submit your claim.
4. **Escalate if necessary:** If the repair costs exceed $2500, or if the owner refuses to pay you back, you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring them to carry out the repairs or cover the cost [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**Next step:** Notify the owner/agent in writing that you are arranging a suitably qualified tradesperson to fix the urgent water issue immediately due to their failure to act, and request reimbursement up to $2500 upon completion.

Based on the current law in force today (5 November 2026), here is how your situation is handled:

**Document & Version Applied:** *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised Version No. 009 (rt-regs-2021-v009), effective 30 June 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### What the Law Says
Under the current regulations, a rental provider **cannot** simply demand professional cleaning or a receipt from a professional cleaner just because it is written in your lease [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The law explicitly states that a provider may only require professional cleaning if:
* Professional cleaning was carried out immediately before your tenancy started and you were advised of this; OR
* Professional cleaning is strictly necessary to restore the premises to the same condition they were in at the start of your tenancy, taking into account the condition report and **fair wear and tear** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

Because you have cleaned the carpets yourself and returned them to their original state (accounting for fair wear and tear), you are **not legally required to pay for a professional cleaner**. The legal obligation is to restore the premises to their original condition, not to use a specific service provider [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### What You Can Do or Ask For
To protect yourself from unfair demands or bond claims, take these steps:
* **Reference the Condition Report:** Use the official condition report you signed at the start of your tenancy as your primary evidence for the state of the "floor coverings" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 
* **Provide Dated Photos:** Submit dated photos you took when you moved in alongside new photos showing the carpets are clean and undamaged (beyond fair wear and tear) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
* **Request a Final Inspection:** Ask to attend the final inspection so you can verify the condition of the premises yourself before the agent completes their section of the condition report [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 
* **Cite "Fair Wear and Tear":** Remind the agent that regulations explicitly state they must allow for fair wear and tear, which does not count as damage caused by the renter [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

Based on the current law in force today, here is your guidance:

**Document & Version Applied**
*Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, version 005 (Authorised by the Chief Parliamentary Counsel), in force from 25 November 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

### What the Law Says
Under Victorian tenancy law, your rental provider has a strict duty to maintain the premises in good repair and in a fit condition for occupation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). You are also entitled to quiet enjoyment of the property [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Damage caused by third parties (like burglars) does not transfer the repair responsibility to you; however, you do have specific duties to report it promptly.

### Your Options & Next Steps

**1. Notify the Provider in Writing Immediately**
You must notify your rental provider in writing as soon as practicable about the fact that damage has occurred and its nature [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). You can send this via electronic communication (e.g., email) in accordance with the *Electronic Transactions (Victoria) Act 2000* [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**2. Pursue Urgent Repairs for Plumbing & Wiring**
If the damaged plumbing or wiring causes a failure of an essential service provided by the landlord (such as hot water, cooking, heating, or laundering facilities), this is legally classified as an **urgent repair** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 
*   The provider must carry out these repairs immediately after being notified [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
*   If you take reasonable steps to get them to act and they fail to do so, you may arrange for a suitably qualified person to fix it yourself and claim reimbursement of up to **$2,500** directly from the provider [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
*   If the repair costs exceed $2,500, or if the provider refuses to pay, you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring them to carry out the repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

**3. Pursue Non-Urgent Repairs**
For any other damage that does not affect essential services, it is classified as a **non-urgent repair** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The provider must complete these within a reasonable time. If they do not fix the issue within **14 days** of receiving your written notice, you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring them to do the work [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

**4. End the Lease Early (If Uninhabitable)**
If the burglary damage is severe enough that the premises are effectively "destroyed or unfit for habitation," you may be entitled to give formal notice to vacate the property early under section 91ZD of the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). If you end the agreement on this basis, the provider **cannot** claim compensation from you for rent foregone [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

**5. Cleaning Obligations**
Regarding your inability to clean: You are generally only required to professionally clean at the end of a tenancy if professional cleaning was done immediately before you moved in, or if it is strictly necessary to restore the property to its original condition accounting for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Because the damage and resulting mess were caused by burglars (not you), you are not liable for restoring that specific damage, and the provider's duty to maintain the premises in good repair covers this [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

**6. Security & Locks**
Ensure the property meets rental minimum standards for locks. External doors must have functioning deadlocks or a locking device operated by a key from the outside [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). If security was compromised during the break-ins, you can request the provider to rectify the locks immediately to restore your right to quiet enjoyment [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

A "suitably qualified person" includes a tradesperson who is registered or licensed for the relevant work, where that work requires it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

The provision covers damage by the renter or visitors, not by burglars, so the documents don't say whether burglary damage counts against you.
- **Your duty to report damage:** You must give the provider written notice "as soon as practicable" of the fact and nature of any damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Electronic notice is allowed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs:** You may arrange urgent repairs if you took reasonable steps to get the provider to do them immediately and couldn't [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Urgent repairs include failure of an essential service for hot water, cooking, heating or laundering [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). A "burst water service" and "flood damage" are given as examples of urgent repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Reimbursement:** If you do the repairs, you must give the provider 7 days' written notice of the repairs and their cost, and the provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The provider is liable only for the reasonable cost or the prescribed amount, whichever is less [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations state the amount is up to $2500 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Who may do the work:** Only a suitably qualified person may do urgent or non-urgent repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Non-urgent repairs:** Give written notice. If the provider hasn't repaired within 14 days, you may apply to VCAT [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Cleaning:** You must leave the premises as far as practicable reasonably clean and in the condition they were in when you moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The provider cannot require professional cleaning unless it was done at the start of the tenancy or is needed to restore the premises to their starting condition, having regard to the condition report [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## Your options before the lease ends

1. **Give written notice now.** Describe the burglary damage to the plumbing and wiring, and the cleaning problem, and attach dated photos. This satisfies the notice duties [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
2. **Request urgent repairs in writing if the plumbing is affected.** Ask for immediate repair and list an emergency contact [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). If the provider doesn't act, you may arrange repairs through a suitably qualified person [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Keep receipts, and send the 7-day written notice of cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Go to VCAT if the provider won't act or pay.** You can apply for an urgent repairs order if you can't meet the cost, the cost exceeds the prescribed amount, or the provider refuses to reimburse [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Tribunal must hear the application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **For non-urgent wiring or other repairs,** wait 14 days after notice, then apply to VCAT. VCAT must hear the application within 7 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). It may consider whether the repairs were needed because of your act or omission [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. **Rent withholding is only through VCAT.** If you've given notice requiring repairs and the provider has failed to comply, you may apply to have rent paid into the Rent Special Account [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
6. **Watch for a repair notice.** A provider may issue a repair notice requiring you to fix damage only if the damage resulted from your failure to take care under the damage duty [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Respond within 14 days if you get one [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Your evidence that the damage was caused by burglars is relevant here.
7. **Cleaning.** Document what you tried and why it can't be done. Don't agree to professional cleaning unless the conditions above are met [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
8. **Safety.** Tell the provider about any defect that could threaten safety [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Keep the condition report and photos for later disputes [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

- **Prescribed matters:** The Regulations prescribe "rent payment (other than payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act)" and "failed payments". - **Electronic payment facilities:** A separate rule says a person must not demand or receive a charge for "the establishment or use of direct debit facilities or any other electronic payment facility for payment of rent" (s 51(3)(b)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

Section 51A is a separate prohibition [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Disclosure:** The provider or agent must tell you about any costs, including third party transaction fees and other electronic payment facility fees, before you consent to a payment method (s 42(7)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Condition of the premises.** The provider must ensure the premises are "provided and maintained" in good repair and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation. This applies even if the renter knew of the disrepair before moving in (s 68(1), (1A)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Minimum standards.** The premises must meet the rental minimum standards on or before the day you enter (s 65A(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Those standards require the premises to be "structurally sound and weatherproof". They also require each room to be "free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Vacant and clean.** The provider must also ensure the premises are vacant and reasonably clean on the agreed day. If they aren't, you aren't required to enter, and you don't pay rent from the agreed day until you actually enter (s 65(1)–(3)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This only covers vacancy and cleanliness, so it doesn't clearly cover damp, mould or rot.

## Your options

**1. Cancel before moving in.** An agreement ends if the renter has not entered into possession and gives notice of termination on the ground that the premises are:
- not in good repair;
- unfit for human habitation;
- not meeting any rental minimum standards; or
- for any other reason unavailable for occupation (s 91L) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

The retrieved text doesn't say whether collecting the keys counts as "entering into possession". Check that point before relying on s 91L.

**2. Cancel after moving in.** You can give a notice of intention to vacate if the premises are unfit for human habitation, or destroyed or unsafe. The termination date can be the date of the notice or later (s 91ZD) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Otherwise, a general notice must give at least 28 days (s 91Z), and on a fixed-term agreement it has no effect if the termination date is before the end of the term (s 91ZA(1)(b)) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**3. Ask for repairs.**
- **Urgent repairs.** These include "the presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure", any fault making the premises unsafe, and any failure to comply with rental minimum standards [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If the premises don't comply on or just after the day you enter, you can request urgent repairs (s 65A(2)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Doing the repairs yourself.** If you've taken reasonable steps to get the provider to act and can't, you may arrange urgent repairs. You must give 7 days' written notice of the repairs and their cost, and the provider must reimburse you within 7 days (s 72) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). - **VCAT for urgent repairs.** You can apply if you can't meet the cost, the cost exceeds the prescribed amount, or the provider refuses to pay. VCAT must hear it within 2 business days (s 73) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Non-urgent repairs.** Give written notice (s 72AA) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If the repairs aren't done within 14 days, you can apply to the Director to investigate (s 74) or to VCAT (s 75). VCAT must hear a s 75 application within 7 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **VCAT orders.** VCAT can order specified repairs by a suitably qualified person, within a set time, plus compensation under s 212(2) (s 76) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The text of s 212 wasn't retrieved, so I can't say how compensation works.

**4. Lower rent.** The retrieved provisions give no right to demand a reduced rent because of defects at the start of a residential rental agreement. The closest options are:
- You don't pay rent until you enter if the premises aren't vacant and reasonably clean (s 65(3)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- After you give repair notice and the provider fails to repair, VCAT must order your rent paid into the Rent Special Account unless the provider shows financial hardship (s 77(2)). If the breach is of s 68 or the minimum standards and the repairs still aren't done by the end of that period, you can apply for that rent to be paid to you (s 77(4)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Compensation may be ordered under s 76(1)(c) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Practical steps

- **Record the defects.** Photograph them, and note them on the condition report. The provider must give you the report before you move in, and you can complete your own (s 35). A condition report given to the provider counts as notice of the defects (s 36(1A)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Correct the report if needed.** You can apply to VCAT to amend an inaccurate condition report within 30 days after the agreement commences (s 35A) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Check the disclosures.** Before the agreement, the provider must disclose whether the premises comply with the minimum standards, and any repair notice about structural mould or damp in the last 3 years (reg 16(2)(b)–(c)) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

  1. You have taken reasonable steps to get the rental provider or their agent to carry out the repairs immediately.
  2. You are unable to get them to do it.
- **The owner's preference for their own tradespeople doesn't change this.** The test in the Act is whether you could get the provider or agent to carry out the repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Act says a suitably qualified person includes a registered or licensed tradesperson where the work requires it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). So hire a licensed plumber rather than fixing it yourself.

2. **Document your attempts.** Record when you contacted the emergency contact, what they said, and that no one could attend.
3. **Arrange a licensed plumber** if the provider's tradespeople still can't come [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Give written notice of the repair and its cost.** You must give the provider 7 days' written notice of the repairs carried out and the cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

# Burglary damage to plumbing and wiring during a Victorian tenancy

I used the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf". Its metadata gives version 115, in force from 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I also used the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, file "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf", version 009, in force from 30 June 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). No later version came up in my search. The documents don't use the words "Authorised Version No.", so the version numbers above come from their metadata.

## What the law says

- **Urgent repairs:** The Act's definition includes a burst water service, a dangerous electrical fault, and "any fault or damage that makes rented premises… unsafe or insecure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Burglary damage to plumbing and wiring may fall within these, depending on the actual damage.
- **Your duty to report:** You must give the rental provider written notice of damage as soon as practicable after becoming aware of it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Cleaning:** At the end of the tenancy you must leave the premises reasonably clean "as far as practicable" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If the damage stops you cleaning, this wording helps you, but the documents don't say how a Tribunal would apply it to your situation.
- **Fault for the damage:** You must not intentionally or negligently damage the premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A provider can only give a repair notice if the damage came from your failure to take care [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A provider can claim on the bond for damage caused by the renter or a renter's visitor [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A visitor means someone on the premises with the renter's permission [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and burglars wouldn't be that.
- **Lease-ending provisions:** A renter may give notice of intention to vacate if the premises are "unfit for human habitation" or "destroyed totally or to such an extent as to be rendered unsafe". The termination date can be the date of the notice or later [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask for

1. **Notify the rental provider in writing now.** Describe the damage and ask for urgent repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **If they don't act, arrange the repairs yourselves.** You can do this if you've taken reasonable steps to get the provider to do them immediately and they haven't [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
   - Give the provider 7 days' written notice of the repairs and their cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
   - The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost, up to the prescribed amount, within 7 days of the notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
   - The standard-form agreement summary gives that amount as $2500 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). I didn't retrieve the operative regulation setting it.
3. **Apply to VCAT for an urgent repairs order.** You can do this if you can't meet the cost, the cost exceeds the prescribed amount, or the provider refuses to pay. VCAT must hear it within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Leave early if the premises are unfit or unsafe.** Give a notice of intention to vacate under s 91ZD [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
   - Whether the damage meets that threshold is a factual question the documents don't answer.
   - For a fixed-term agreement of more than 5 years, the standard form says the provider can't claim lost rent if you leave on this ground [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say the same for shorter agreements.
   - The ordinary notice-of-intention-to-vacate rule requires at least 28 days' notice. For fixed terms it has no effect if the termination date falls before the end of the term [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. **Raise the repeated break-ins and locks.** The standard agreement requires the provider to ensure window locks and deadlocks that meet the rental minimum standards [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). If the provider unreasonably withholds consent to a lock change, you can apply to VCAT for a determination that consent isn't required [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't cover

They don't address who bears the cost of burglary damage, insurance, or reporting to police. For your specific fixed term and any lease-break consequences, check your own agreement and consider advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria or a community legal centre.

[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

If you have taken reasonable steps to arrange this but cannot get them to act, you may arrange urgent repairs yourself. You must then give **7 days’ written notice** of the repairs and their cost; the provider is liable to reimburse the reasonable cost, up to any prescribed limit, within **7 days** after receiving that notice. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

### Can the app charge you a card fee?
**Yes, provided a fee-free alternative is available.**

### Does it matter who receives the fee (the app vs. the agent)?
**Yes, it matters legally.** 
The law draws a clear line between third-party fees and fees charged directly by the rental provider or their agent:
* **Third-party app fees:** Fees charged by an external payment processor are permitted, provided a fee-free alternative is available and you are informed of the cost beforehand [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* **Fees charged by the provider/agent:** Under section 51(3)(b) of the Act, a rental provider or their agent is strictly prohibited from demanding or receiving any charge for the establishment or use of direct debit or other electronic payment facilities themselves [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

The rental provider has a strict duty to ensure the premises comply with these minimum standards, are vacant and reasonably clean when you move in, and are maintained in good repair and a fit condition for occupation [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**Your Options**
*Can I cancel?*
Yes. The *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* provides a specific pathway for "Termination by renter before possession" under Section 91L if the premises do not meet minimum standards or are unfit for habitation [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You should photograph the damp, mould, and rotting timber immediately and notify your provider in writing that you cannot take possession due to these breaches.

*Can I ask for repairs?*
Yes. You must notify the rental provider in writing as soon as practicable about the damage [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
- If the issues are classified as **urgent repairs** (e.g., structural failures or safety hazards), the provider must carry them out immediately upon notification [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- For **non-urgent repairs**, if the provider does not act within 14 days of receiving your written notice, you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring them to complete the work [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

*Can I ask for lower rent?*
You cannot unilaterally reduce your rent. However, if the provider fails to fix the issues, you can apply to VCAT for an order authorising you to pay your rent into a **Rent Special Account** instead of directly to the provider [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Tribunal will only grant this if satisfied the provider has breached their maintenance duties and cannot demonstrate financial hardship [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Additionally, VCAT can order the provider to pay you compensation for any losses suffered [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Authorised Version No. 115)** and the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (Authorised Version No. 009)**, which are in force today:

### Do you have to pay for a professional cleaner?
**No, not automatically.** Under Victorian law, a rental provider cannot require you to professionally clean your carpets (or pay for it) unless that cleaning is actually necessary to restore the carpets to the exact condition they were in when you moved in, after accounting for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). 

If your lease contains a blanket clause demanding professional cleaning regardless of the actual state of the carpets, that specific term may be invalid. The law prohibits tenancy agreements from including terms that require professional cleaning at the end of a tenancy unless it is contained within the standard form agreement and is strictly tied to restoring the premises to their initial condition [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 

Since you have cleaned the carpets yourself and they are back to how they were when you moved in (minus any fair wear and tear), professional cleaning has not become "required" under the law. You only have a legal duty to leave the premises reasonably clean and in the same condition as when you entered, accounting for fair wear and tear [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What helps show the carpets' condition?
To prove you have met your obligation and protect your bond, you should rely on the following evidence:
* **The Condition Report:** You are entitled to a condition report at the start of your tenancy, which records the state of all fixtures and fittings (including floor coverings) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Compare the agent's final assessment against your signed copy of this report. 
* **Dated Photos:** The law explicitly advises renters to take photos at both the beginning and the end of the tenancy to show the condition of items and fixtures [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Dated, close-up, and wide-angle photos of the carpets are highly effective evidence in any dispute.
* **Fair Wear and Tear:** Remember that "fair wear and tear" does not count as damage or dirt you are responsible for [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If the carpets have naturally faded or worn over time, the agent cannot charge you to restore them to a pristine, move-in condition.

If the agent still tries to claim from your bond for professional cleaning despite the carpets being clean and matching the initial condition report, they must provide evidence that does not conflict with your signed condition report [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You can dispute this through the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority (RTBA) or apply to VCAT if necessary.
