Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997** (Authorised Version No. 115, in force from 2026-10-13) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), here are your options while the lease is still active:

### 1. Report the damage immediately
You must give written notice to your residential rental provider as soon as practicable after becoming aware of the damage or breakdown of facilities [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This notice must clearly state both the fact that the damage occurred and its nature [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You can send this electronically in accordance with the *Electronic Transactions (Victoria) Act 2000* [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### 2. Arrange urgent repairs
Damaged plumbing and wiring likely qualify as **urgent repairs**. You have two pathways to get them fixed:
* **Apply to VCAT:** If you cannot afford the repairs or if the cost exceeds the prescribed amount, you may apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring your provider to carry out the repairs. The Tribunal must hear urgent repair applications within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* **Do it yourself and claim reimbursement:** If you have taken reasonable steps to get your provider (or their agent) to fix the issue immediately but they haven't, you may arrange the repairs yourself. You must give your provider written notice of the repairs and the cost at least 7 days before carrying them out. Your provider is then liable to reimburse you for the reasonable cost within 7 days of receiving that notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### 3. Terminate the lease early (if uninhabitable)
If the burglary damage is severe enough that the premises are **"unfit for human habitation"** or have been **"destroyed totally or to such an extent as to be rendered unsafe,"** you may give your provider a notice of intention to vacate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
* The termination date on this notice can be the day you give it, or a later date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* This allows you to end the lease early without being penalised for breaking the fixed term.

### 4. Liability for the burglary damage
Under Victorian tenancy law, a residential rental provider is only entitled to claim from your bond for damage **"caused by the renter or a renter's visitor"** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Because the damage was caused by burglars (third parties), you are not liable for these repairs, and your bond cannot be used to cover them. You remain responsible only for keeping the premises reasonably clean and in the same condition as when you moved in, accounting for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**Recommended next steps:** 
1. Send written notice of the damage and its nature to your provider today.
2. If the plumbing/wiring issues prevent basic living or pose a safety risk, contact VCAT immediately for an urgent repair order, or arrange repairs yourself if you can afford them upfront.
3. If the property is genuinely uninhabitable, issue a notice of intention to vacate under section 91ZD.

**Short answer:** You don't have to wait for the owner's tradespeople. The law lets you arrange urgent repairs yourself in some circumstances, but the repairer must be suitably qualified, and you must give written notice and keep the costs reasonable.

**Which version applies:** The most recent Regulations text I retrieved is the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised Version **009**, which has an in-force date of 30 June 2026 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Its urgent-repairs section wasn't in the excerpt I could retrieve, so I've relied on the previous version, Authorised Version 005 (in force 25 November 2025 to 9 February 2026) [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The latest *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* I retrieved is Authorised Version 110, which ended on 24 November 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The documents don't include the Act version in force today, so please check the current text before relying on this.

**What the law says**

- **Urgent repairs:** Water supply failure counts. The definition covers "a failure or breakdown of the gas, electricity or water supply to rented premises" and "a burst water service" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa097%20authorised.pdf). This definition comes from the 2021 Act text [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa097%20authorised.pdf), so I can't confirm it is unchanged. The documents don't say whether a broken tap alone qualifies, or whether turning off the whole house's water makes it urgent.
- **Your right to arrange repairs:** You may arrange urgent repairs if you have taken reasonable steps to get the landlord or agent to carry out the repairs immediately, and you are unable to get them to do so [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Qualified repairers only:** Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, both urgent and non-urgent [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- **Cost limit:** The landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost of the repairs, up to $2,500 under the 2025 Regulations [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The Act says the landlord is liable for the reasonable cost or the prescribed amount, whichever is less [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Notify in writing now.** Renters must give written notice to the landlord as soon as practicable after becoming aware of a breakdown of facilities [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Send this to the emergency contact, and keep a copy.
2. **Document your attempts.** Keep a record of your attempts to reach the owner or their tradespeople, since you must show reasonable steps and that you could not get the repairs done [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
3. **Arrange a suitably qualified plumber.** Get a quote and keep the invoice.
4. **Give written notice of the repair and its cost.** You must give the landlord 7 days' written notice of the repairs carried out and the cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The landlord must reimburse you within 7 days after receiving that notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
5. **If the owner refuses to pay or the cost is too high,** you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring the landlord to carry out the urgent repairs, if you cannot meet the cost, the cost exceeds the prescribed amount, or the landlord refuses to pay [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). VCAT must hear the application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover:** They don't say whether an owner's requirement to use only their own tradespeople overrides your right to arrange urgent repairs. They also don't confirm whether a broken tap, as opposed to a burst pipe or a whole-house supply failure, is urgent. For a definite answer, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria (consumer.vic.gov.au/urgentrepairs) or VCAT.

**Short answer:** Not automatically. Under the current regulations, the clause can only require professional cleaning if it is needed to restore the carpets to their move-in condition, and fair wear and tear is taken into account. ## What the law says

- The governing instrument is the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version version 009** (in force from 30 June 2026). It is the most recent version I found [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The Act version I retrieved, the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* version 110, shows an end date of 24 November 2025 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), so I could not confirm the current Act version.
- Regulation 12(1) says the landlord **must not require** you to arrange professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy **unless** either:
  - (a) professional cleaning was done before the tenancy started and you were told so; or
  - (b) professional cleaning **is required to restore the premises to the same condition** they were in immediately before the tenancy started, **having regard to the condition report and taking into account fair wear and tear** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- Regulation 12(2) is the prescribed term that lets the renter be made to pay for professional cleaning, but only "if professional cleaning becomes required to restore the premises" to that move-in condition, again having regard to the condition report and fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- Under the Act, a clause requiring professional cleaning at the end of a tenancy is prohibited unless it is in the standard form [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Section 27C allows the standard form to include this kind of term [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- A renter may apply to VCAT for an order declaring invalid or varying a term that is harsh or unconscionable [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

1. **Check the two conditions.** Look at your condition report from move-in. Did it record carpets as clean? Was professional cleaning done before you moved in, and were you told? If the answer to the second is no, the landlord's requirement is weaker.
2. **Ask the agent in writing** which of the two conditions they say applies, and what they say is required to restore the carpets to the move-in condition. Note that the regulation requires the assessment to take account of fair wear and tear.
3. **Gather evidence of the carpets' condition:**
   - The move-in condition report and any photos or videos from move-in.
   - Your own photos or video of the carpets at move-out, dated and showing the whole room.
   - Your cleaning receipts, the method and products used, and the date.
   - Any agent inspection report or correspondence.
4. **If the dispute continues,** you can apply to VCAT under the harsh or unconscionable terms provision [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The documents I found don't say how VCAT would weigh your evidence, so check VCAT's guidance.

## What the documents don't cover

- They don't say what evidence VCAT would accept as proof of carpet condition.
- They don't say whether the agent can deduct cleaning costs from your bond, or how a bond claim is handled.
- I could not check whether your lease is in the standard form, which affects whether the clause is valid.

## What the law says

- **Cleaning costs are a bond claim matter.** A landlord is entitled to claim from the bond "the reasonable cost of cleaning any part of the premises, if the premises were not left reasonably clean by the renter, having regard to the condition of the premises at the commencement of the residential rental agreement" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The renter's duty.** At the end of a tenancy, the renter must leave the premises, as far as practicable, "reasonably clean" and in the same condition as when they moved in, taking fair wear and tear into account. This comes from section 63 as it appears in Authorised Version No. 98 (dated 29 March 2021), so I could not confirm the current wording from Version 115 [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa098%20authorised.pdf).
- **Evidence before a claim.** At least 3 days before a bond claim is made to the landlord, the landlord or their agent "must give each renter bond claim evidence that supports the claim." Bond claim evidence includes "an invoice," "a receipt," "a quote," or "a photograph" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). That evidence "must not conflict with a statement in a condition report" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Claim form.** A landlord must not get a renter's signature on a claim form unless it specifies the amount of bond to be refunded and any apportionment [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Notice of claims.** If a claim is made without the consent of all parties, the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority must notify the other parties. The notice must state that the Authority will pay the claim unless, within 14 days, a party gives written notice that the claim is subject to a Tribunal application [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't cover

- Whether agreeing to a bond deduction counts as agreeing to pay an invoice. None of the retrieved documents addresses this.

The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person and 400 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Can the app charge you the card fee?

The documents don't give a clear yes or no.

- Section 42(7) assumes some payment methods carry fees, as long as you are told first [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Section 51(3)(b) bans charges for using "any other electronic payment facility" for rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A card payment through an app could fall within those words, but the documents don't say whether a card surcharge counts.
- Section 51A depends on what is "prescribed". The prescribed matters are in the regulations, which I didn't retrieve, so I can't say whether a card fee is caught [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Does it matter who gets the fee?

- **The duties in s 42(4) and (7) bind the provider or their agent** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The app company is not named, so those duties apply to it only if it acts as the agent.
- **The bans in s 51(3) and s 51A apply to "a person"** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). They are not limited to the provider or agent. On the wording, a fee going to the app company is not automatically outside them.
- **The only exception in the text I have is for an ADI under s 51A** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The excerpt doesn't define "ADI", so I can't say whether the app company qualifies.

## What you can do

- Use the free bank transfer. The agent must keep a no-cost method reasonably available [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Ask the agent or provider, before you agree to card payment, to state in writing every cost of that method (s 42(7)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Ask who receives the fee and what the agent says it is for.
- If you've already paid a card fee, raise s 51(3)(b) and s 51A with the agent in writing.
- You and the provider can agree to change how rent is paid (s 42(6)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

The retrieved documents don't cover complaint or enforcement steps, or the regulations that define "prescribed" fees. For a firm answer on your app's card fee, check those or get advice from a tenancy advice service.

answer:
**The documents I retrieved do not include the version of the law in force today (6 November 2026), so I can't name its Authorised Version number.**

- The most recent Act I found is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* in "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf" (version 110, dated 6 August 2025). Its metadata says it was in force from 2025-08-06 to 2025-11-24 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The most recent regulations I found are the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* in "rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf" (version 005, dated 25 November 2025). They were in force from 2025-11-25 to 2026-02-09 [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- Both ended before today, so what follows describes the law as it stood in those versions. Check it against the current version before relying on it.

My second search failed, so I did not retrieve the text of the section on ending a lease for unfit premises (s 91ZD) or the rental minimum standards themselves.

## What the law says

- **Condition on moving in.** The provider must make sure the premises are vacant and reasonably clean on the agreed move-in day. If they aren't, you don't have to move in. You also don't pay rent from the agreed day until you actually move in (s 65) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). That section covers vacancy and cleanliness only. It doesn't mention damp or rot.
- **Rental minimum standards.** The provider must make sure the premises meet the prescribed rental minimum standards on or before the day you move in (s 65A(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The standards are prescribed elsewhere, and I did not retrieve them.
- **Good repair.** The Act also refers to the provider's duty to keep the premises in good repair (s 68) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), and the standard-form agreement says the provider must keep them in a fit condition for occupation [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- **Mould and damp as urgent repairs.** The 2018 amending text in an older version (v088, dated 2 July 2019) added "the presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure" to the urgent repairs definition in s 3(1) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). I did not see the current definition, so confirm it.

## What you can do

**1. Ask for repairs**
- If the premises don't meet the minimum standards on or immediately after move-in day, you can send the provider a request for urgent repairs (s 65A(2)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- For other repairs, give written notice. If the provider hasn't done them within 14 days, you can apply to the Director to investigate (s 74) or go to the Tribunal (s 75). The Tribunal must hear a non-urgent application within 7 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- For urgent repairs, you can arrange them yourself if you took reasonable steps to get the provider to do them immediately and couldn't. Give 7 days' written notice of the repairs and cost. The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost, up to the prescribed amount, within 7 days of that notice (s 72) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The regulations form puts the reimbursement cap at $2500 [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- You can apply to the Tribunal for an urgent repairs order if you can't meet the cost, the cost is above the prescribed amount, or the provider refuses to pay. It must hear this within 2 business days (s 73) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The Tribunal can order specified repairs by a suitably qualified person, with a deadline, and can order compensation under s 212(2) (s 76) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). I did not retrieve s 212.
- A condition report that lists defects counts as notice of them to the provider (s 36(1A)). You can fill one in yourself if you weren't given one, and you have 5 business days after moving in to return it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Putting the mould and rot in writing now helps either way.

**2. Ask for lower rent**
- The retrieved text has no provision letting you simply reduce the rent.
- What it does provide is that, after giving repair notice, you can ask the Tribunal to let you pay rent into the Rent Special Account. The Tribunal must make the order if the provider failed to do the repairs and hasn't shown financial hardship (s 77) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- Rent is not waived under that order. It is held, and paid to the provider at the end of the period. You can apply to have it paid to you if the provider still hasn't done required repairs for a breach of s 68 or the minimum standards [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The compensation power in s 76(1)(c) may also be relevant [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**3. Cancel**
- Section 65(2) lets you refuse to move in only for vacancy or cleanliness problems [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The regulations' standard form refers to a renter giving notice of intention to vacate under s 91ZD "on the basis the premises are destroyed or unfit for habitation". In that case the provider can't claim rent foregone [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). I did not retrieve s 91ZD itself, so I can't say whether damp, mould and rotting timber qualify or what the notice requires.
- The form also says nothing stops you applying to VCAT for a compensation order if the other party breaches the agreement (cl 16.4(c)) [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

**Next step.** Because I couldn't retrieve the current version or s 91ZD, check the in-force Act on legislation.vic.gov.au. You could also contact Consumer Affairs Victoria or VCAT before deciding whether to cancel.

**Short answer:** The retrieved documents don't say you must wait for the owner's tradespeople. They also don't say you can hire anyone you like. Whether you can arrange the repair yourself depends on the steps below, and on whether a broken tap counts as an "urgent repair". I couldn't confirm that last point.

## Which documents I relied on
- **Current document:** *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised Version 009 (file rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30), in force from 30 June 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). It has been superseded, so I can't confirm the Act's current wording. I'm using it only to show how section 72 read in that version.

## What the law says
- **Renter's right:** A renter may arrange urgent repairs if they have taken reasonable steps to get the rental provider or agent to carry out the repairs immediately, and they are unable to get the provider or agent to do so [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The current regulations' summary says the same thing [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Who does the work:** The current regulations' rights summary says only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, urgent or non-urgent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). I found nothing in the retrieved documents that lets a rental provider limit repairs to their own tradespeople.
- **Reimbursement:** Under the current regulations' summary, a renter who arranges urgent repairs may be reimbursed by the rental provider for the reasonable cost, up to $2500 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Applying to VCAT:** You can apply to VCAT for an order requiring the rental provider to carry out urgent repairs if [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf):
  - you can't meet the cost;
  - the cost is more than $2500; or
  - the rental provider refuses to pay.

## What you can do
1. **Press the urgent request.** Tell the emergency contact and the rental provider or agent, ideally in writing, that the repair is urgent and that you can't wait for their tradespeople. Keep a record. Your own steps to get them to act immediately count as "reasonable steps" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
2. **If they still can't act immediately,** you may arrange the repair yourself, using a suitably qualified person [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The retrieved documents don't say how long you must wait before doing this.
3. **Get written notice and costs to the rental provider.** In Version 110 of the Act (superseded), the renter had to give 7 days' written notice of the repairs and their cost. The rental provider then had to reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days of receiving that notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). I can't confirm these periods apply today.
4. **If they refuse or you can't pay,** apply to VCAT. In Version 110, VCAT had to hear an urgent repairs application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). I can't confirm that is still the rule.

## What the documents don't answer
- **Is a broken tap an "urgent repair"?** The regulations point to the definition in section 3(1) of the Act, which I didn't retrieve [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The only plumbing example in the documents is a "burst water service" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Don't assume a tap qualifies. A tap that has forced you to shut off water to the whole house may well qualify, but check the definition.

- **Which form applies to you.** The rights summary I could read in full in the current regulations comes from Form 2, for agreements of more than 5 years [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Your agreement may use a different form.

**Short answer:** Under the current law, the agent can't require a professional cleaning receipt just because the lease says so. A professional clean can only be required if one is actually needed to restore the carpets to their starting condition. The documents don't mention pets, so I can't say whether a pet clause is treated differently.

**Documents used (in force today, 6 Nov 2026)**
- *rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf*, the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, version 115, in force from 13 October 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- *rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf*, the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, version 009, in force from 30 June 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

I'm taking the version numbers from the documents' metadata, not from text in the documents.

## What the law says

- **Extra cleaning clauses are generally prohibited.** A lease must not include a term requiring professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy, or requiring the renter to pay for it, unless that term is in the standard form [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 27B(1)(d)–(e)). A prohibited term is void and unenforceable [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 26A(2)).
- **The standard-form term is conditional.** A lease may include a term for professional cleaning only if it becomes required to restore the premises to their condition immediately before the tenancy started, taking into account fair wear and tear [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 27C(1)).
- **The Regulations set the same test.** The rental provider must not require professional cleaning, or cleaning to a professional standard, unless:
  - (a) it was carried out immediately before the tenancy started and you were told so; or
  - (b) it is required to restore the premises to the same condition they were in at the start, having regard to the condition report and taking into account fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) (reg 12(1)).
- **Your duty to pay is also conditional.** You must have the premises professionally cleaned, or pay for it, only if cleaning becomes required to restore them to their starting condition, again having regard to the condition report and fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) (reg 12(2)).

**Applied to you:** If the carpets are back to their move-in condition (allowing for fair wear and tear), professional cleaning isn't "required". On that basis a receipt shouldn't be demanded. The one exception to check is (a). If the carpets were professionally cleaned before you moved in and you were told, the agent has a stronger argument.

## What you can do or ask

- **Rely on the condition report.** The test is judged "having regard to the condition report" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). You should have been given 2 copies (or one emailed copy) on or before move-in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Compare it with the carpets' current state.
- **Ask the agent to identify the problem.** Ask them to point to what in the carpets needs professional cleaning to match the condition report, and to confirm whether the carpets were professionally cleaned before your tenancy.
- **Apply to the Tribunal if needed.** A renter can apply to have a lease term declared invalid or varied if it is harsh or unconscionable [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 28).

**Not covered:** The documents don't say what other evidence helps, such as dated photos or videos, or whether a receipt is ever required. The condition report is the only evidence they name. Photos of the carpets at move-out are a sensible extra, but that suggestion is mine, not from the documents.

answer:
## Which law applies

The Act in force today (6 November 2026) is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file **rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf**, labelled **version 115**, in force from 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The retrieved text doesn't print an "Authorised Version No." line, so I'm relying on the version number in the file's metadata. For the $ figures and standard-form wording I used **rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf** (Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, version 009, in force from 30 June 2026) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Tell the provider in writing.** You must give written notice "as soon as practicable" after you become aware of damage to the premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Email counts [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The provider's repair duty.** The standard agreement terms say the rental provider "must maintain the premises in good repair and in a fit condition for occupation" [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Your cleaning duty is limited.** At the end of the agreement you must leave the premises reasonably clean "as far as practicable" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). That wording is relevant because the damage is stopping you from cleaning properly.
- **Burglar damage is not automatically your fault.** A repair notice to a renter is only available where the damage was caused by the renter's failure to comply with s 61(1). That section covers damage a renter or visitor causes intentionally or negligently [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask for

1. **Give written notice of the break-ins and damage now**, and keep documentary evidence. The Tribunal considers whether the provider was notified and whether you provided documentary evidence of the repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask for urgent repairs.**
   - You may arrange urgent repairs yourself only if you first took reasonable steps to get the provider or agent to do them immediately and couldn't [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
   - You must then give 7 days' written notice of the repairs and the cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
   - The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days of that notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
   - The reimbursement is capped at the prescribed amount [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), which the regulations' standard terms give as $2500 [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
   - Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, urgent or non-urgent [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Apply to VCAT (the Tribunal) for an urgent repairs order** if you can't meet the cost, the cost is over the prescribed amount ($2500 per [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)), or the provider refuses to pay [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Tribunal must hear it within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **For non-urgent repairs:**

## What the law says

The current documents are **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version v115 (in force 13 October 2026), Author: Barbara Hargreaves** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version v009 (in force 30 June 2026), Author: Lavina Mandy** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

- The premises must be **structurally sound and weatherproof**, and each room must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- The rental provider must ensure the premises are in **good repair** and reasonably fit and suitable for occupation, even if the renter knew about disrepair before moving in. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- Mould or damp related to the building structure, failure to meet rental minimum standards, and faults or damage making the premises unsafe or insecure are classified as **urgent repairs**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- The rental provider must ensure the premises meet the rental minimum standards **on or before the day you enter into occupation**. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- The Act does **not expressly provide an automatic right to cancel merely because you signed the lease, collected the keys, and then discovered these defects**. The documents do, however, provide the termination options below. [[16]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

### 1. Ask for urgent repairs

Give the rental provider or agent **written notice immediately**, describing the damp, mould and rotting timber, attaching dated photographs, and asking for suitably qualified contractors to investigate and remedy the underlying cause. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Because structural mould or damp and unsafe damage are urgent repairs, the provider must arrange the repairs after being notified. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) If they do not act, you may arrange urgent repairs after taking reasonable steps to have the provider do them immediately; reimbursement may be available for reasonable costs up to **$2,500**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

If you cannot meet the cost, the cost exceeds $2,500, or the provider refuses to reimburse you, you may apply to **VCAT** for an order requiring the urgent repairs. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

### 2. Ask for non-urgent repairs or a VCAT order

The rental provider must also maintain the premises in good repair and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Give written notice and, if the repairs are not completed within **14 days**, you may apply to VCAT for a repairs order. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

### 3. Do not move in if the premises are not fit

If the premises are not vacant and reasonably clean on the agreed occupation day, you are not required to enter into occupation and are not required to pay rent for the period before you actually enter. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The documents do not state that collecting the keys itself removes this protection, but they also do not clearly decide how key collection affects “occupation”; that may depend on the facts.

### 4. Ask for a rent reduction or compensation

You can ask the provider to agree to a temporary rent reduction while the premises are unusable or partly unusable. The documents do not state an automatic percentage reduction or an automatic right to reduce the rent unilaterally. [[16]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

You may apply to VCAT for compensation where the provider failed to comply with the residential rental agreement or statutory duties, or where you paid more than required. [[16]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) VCAT may order compensation, including a **refund or reduction of rent**. [[16]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Do not simply stop paying rent without an agreement or VCAT order.

### 5. End the lease

- If the house is **unfit for human habitation** or has been rendered unsafe, section 91ZD allows you to give a written notice of intention to vacate effective immediately or on a later date. [[16]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- If the provider fails to comply with a VCAT order, you may give at least **14 days’ notice** under section 91ZE. [[16]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- For a fixed-term agreement, successive breaches can support termination after the provider has breached the same duty on two previous occasions and the required breach notices have been given; the notice must specify a termination date at least **14 days** after it is given. [[16]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The documents do not establish that damp, mould and rotting timber automatically make every property “unfit for human habitation.” That will depend on the seriousness and safety impact of the defects.

**Practical next step:** do not move in or pay further rent without first sending written notice, preserving photographs and other evidence, and clearly stating whether you seek immediate repairs, an agreed termination, or a rent reduction. If the provider disputes the condition or refuses to act, apply to VCAT for urgent repairs, compensation, or—if justified—orders supporting termination.

### What the law says
Under Victorian residential tenancy law, a rental provider or their agent **must ensure that a fee-free payment method** (other than your own bank fees) is reasonably available to you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). They are also legally required to give you clear information about any costs you may incur by using a specific payment method—including **"third party transaction fees"**—before you agree to use it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The standard tenancy agreement reinforces this by noting that the provider must permit at least one fee-free option and allow you to use Centrepay or another electronic funds transfer [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

### Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or the agent?
**No.** The law focuses entirely on whether **you** are charged extra, not who collects the money. Because the legislation explicitly calls out "third party transaction fees," a rental provider cannot force you to pay a card fee simply because it is routed through an app rather than their own bank account [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). As long as they provide a genuinely free alternative (like your manual bank transfer option), they are complying with the law, even if the app still charges you for convenience.

### What you can do or ask
* **Use the fee-free method:** Since your app offers a manual bank transfer with no fee, you can simply use that option to avoid the charge entirely.
* **Request written confirmation:** If you are ever unsure whether a payment method is truly free, ask your agent in writing to confirm that the method incurs *"no additional costs (other than bank fees or account fees payable on your bank account)"* [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
* **Check your agreement:** Review your standard tenancy agreement's payment section. It should list your available options and explicitly note that a fee-free method is permitted [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

Based on the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021** (Authorised Version v009, in force from 30 June 2026), here is how the law applies to your situation:

### Do you have to pay for a professional cleaner?
No, not if your DIY cleaning has successfully restored the carpets to their original condition. Under Victorian law, a rental provider **must not require** you to arrange professional cleaning at the end of a tenancy unless one of two conditions is met [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf):
1. Professional cleaning was carried out immediately before you moved in, and you were explicitly advised of this; or
2. Professional cleaning is actually required to restore the premises to the same condition they were in at the start of the tenancy, after accounting for **fair wear and tear** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

Since you have cleaned the carpets yourself and they are back to how they were when you moved in (minus normal fair wear and tear), professional cleaning is not "required" under the law. You cannot be forced to pay for a service that isn't legally necessary to meet your obligations.

### What helps show the carpets' condition?
To prove you have met your cleaning obligations, you should rely on:
* **The signed Condition Report:** This document records the state of the premises (including floor coverings) at the start of your tenancy and is the primary benchmark used to determine if professional cleaning is actually required [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). 
* **Dated photos:** You should take close-up and wide-angle photos of the carpets at both the start and end of your tenancy. These photos must be dated, labelled with the room/location, and attached to or kept alongside the condition report [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). They are explicitly noted as highly useful for resolving disputes over cleaning or damage [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

If the agent still demands a receipt, you can politely decline by pointing out that the law only mandates professional cleaning if it is necessary to restore the premises to their initial state (accounting for fair wear and tear), which your DIY work has already achieved. If they attempt to deduct this from your bond, you would present your signed condition report and dated before/after photos to VCAT as evidence that no professional service was required.

### What the Law Says About This Situation
The retrieved regulations do not contain a specific legal category for "burglary" or "break-ins." Instead, Victorian tenancy law treats this under general obligations regarding damage to the premises and the rental provider's duty to maintain the property [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 
* **Provider's Duty:** The rental provider must maintain the premises in good repair and in a fit condition for occupation at all times [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
* **Renter's Notification Duty:** Wherever damage occurs, you are legally required to notify the rental provider in writing as soon as practicable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
* **End-of-Lease Condition:** You are generally required to leave the premises in the same condition you moved in, excluding "fair wear and tear" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Damage caused by external criminals is not your fault or fair wear and tear, so you should not be held financially responsible for restoring it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

### Your Options Before the Lease Ends
You have several immediate rights and steps you can take to address the plumbing, wiring, and security issues:

**1. Send Written Notice Immediately**
Formally notify your rental provider in writing about the break-ins and all resulting damage (plumbing, wiring, etc.) as soon as practicable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Keep a copy of this notice for your records.

**2. Trigger Urgent Repair Obligations**
If the damaged wiring or plumbing affects essential services (e.g., hot water, cooking, heating, or laundering appliances), it qualifies as an **urgent repair** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 
* The provider must carry out these repairs immediately upon being notified [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
* If you take reasonable steps to contact them and they fail to act, you may arrange the repairs yourself and claim reimbursement for reasonable costs up to **$2,500** directly from the provider [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
* If the repair costs exceed $2,500 or you cannot afford to pay upfront, you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring the provider to carry out the urgent repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

**3. Pursue Non-Urgent Repairs via VCAT**
For damage that does not affect essential services (non-urgent repairs), the provider must complete the work within a reasonable time [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). If they fail to act within **14 days** of receiving your written notice, you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring them to do the repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

**4. Request Security Upgrades**
You have the right to request changes to locks or security devices to prevent further break-ins. The provider must not unreasonably refuse consent if you seek to change a lock in a master key system, and they cannot give keys to anyone excluded from the premises under relevant intervention orders [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

**5. Protect Your Bond & Cleaning Obligations**
Because the damage was caused by burglars, you are not liable for professional cleaning or restoration costs related to it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). At the end of your tenancy, ensure you have photos and the signed condition report from when you moved in to prove that this damage did not exist prior to your occupancy [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

*Note: The provided documents do not contain specific information on claiming compensation for stolen personal belongings or applying for rent reductions due to uninhabitable conditions. For those matters, you would need to consult additional legal resources or VCAT guidelines.*
